# FastAPI Tutorial Notes — Response Models, Forms/Files, Errors, Encoder, Updates

*(all snippets: modern `Annotated` / Python 3.10+ `X | None` style, Pydantic v2)*

---

## 1. `response-model` — Return Type & `response_model`

**Kernidee:** Der Rückgabetyp der Path-Operation-Funktion (`-> Item`) definiert das Response-Modell: FastAPI **validiert**, **serialisiert** (Pydantic/Rust, schnell), **dokumentiert** (JSON Schema in OpenAPI) und vor allem **filtert/begrenzt** die Ausgabedaten auf die deklarierten Felder. Wenn der tatsächlich zurückgegebene Typ nicht dem deklarierten entspricht (dict, ORM-Objekt), nutzt man stattdessen den Decorator-Parameter `response_model=`.

```python
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    return item

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items() -> list[Item]:
    return [Item(name="Portal Gun", price=42.0), Item(name="Plumbus", price=32.0)]
```

### Return-Type-Annotation vs. `response_model=`
- `response_model` ist Parameter des **Decorators** (`@app.get/post/put/delete`), nicht der Funktion.
- Nötig, wenn man z. B. ein `dict` / DB-Objekt zurückgibt, es aber als Pydantic-Modell dokumentieren will — sonst meckern Editor/mypy zu Recht. Trick: Funktionsrückgabe als `Any` annotieren.
- **Priorität:** Sind beide gesetzt, gewinnt `response_model`.
- `response_model` nimmt denselben Typ wie ein Pydantic-Feld: Modell, `list[Item]`, `dict[str, float]`, `Union[...]`.

```python
@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user_in: UserIn):
    ...
```

### Warum Filtern? (Security)
`UserIn` enthält das Klartext-Passwort. Nutzt man dasselbe Modell als Ein- und Ausgabe, gibt die API das Passwort zurück — bei anderen Path Operations schickt man dann fremden Clients Passwörter. **Nie** Klartext-Passwörter speichern oder zurückgeben.

```python
# Anti-Pattern (Doku: "Don't do this in production!")
class UserIn(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

@app.post("/user/")
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> UserIn:   # leakt das Passwort
    return user
```

`EmailStr` braucht `uv add email-validator` (oder `uv add "pydantic[email]"`).

### Return Type + Data Filtering via Vererbung (bevorzugt)
Basisklasse als Return-Typ annotieren, Subklasse zurückgeben → Typcheck ok (Subklasse ist gültiger `BaseUser`), FastAPI filtert trotzdem auf die Felder von `BaseUser`. FastAPI verhindert intern, dass Vererbungsregeln zum Durchreichen zusätzlicher Felder führen.

```python
class BaseUser(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

class UserIn(BaseUser):
    password: str

@app.post("/user/")
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> BaseUser:   # password wird herausgefiltert
    return user
```

### Andere Return-Type-Annotationen
```python
# Response-Subklassen werden automatisch erkannt
async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response: ...
async def get_teleport() -> RedirectResponse: ...
```
Ungültig ist eine Union aus Response und Nicht-Pydantic-Typ (`-> Response | dict`) → FastAPI versucht ein Response-Modell zu bauen und scheitert. Lösung:

```python
@app.get("/portal", response_model=None)
async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response | dict:
    if teleport:
        return RedirectResponse(url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ")
    return {"message": "Here's your interdimensional portal."}
```
`response_model=None` schaltet Validierung/Filterung/Doku für diese Operation ab.

### Encoding-Parameter
```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude_unset=True)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    return items[item_id]
```
- `response_model_exclude_unset=True` → nur explizit gesetzte Werte; Defaults fallen raus. Für `{"name": "Foo", "price": 50.2}` kommt genau das zurück.
- Werte, die **explizit gesetzt** wurden und zufällig dem Default entsprechen, bleiben drin (Pydantic merkt sich "set").
- Weiter: `response_model_exclude_defaults=True`, `response_model_exclude_none=True`.

```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}/name", response_model=Item,
         response_model_include={"name", "description"})
@app.get("/items/{item_id}/public", response_model=Item,
         response_model_exclude={"tax"})
```
- `include`/`exclude` nehmen ein `set[str]`; `list`/`tuple` wird intern zu `set` konvertiert.
- **Nachteil:** Das OpenAPI-JSON-Schema zeigt weiterhin das vollständige Modell → besser mehrere Klassen. Gilt analog für `response_model_by_alias`.

---

## 2. `extra-models` — Mehrere Modelle

**Kernidee:** Eine Entität braucht oft mehrere Modelle: Input mit `password`, Output ohne, DB-Modell mit `hashed_password`. Duplizierung reduziert man per Vererbung von einem `UserBase`.

```python
class UserBase(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

class UserIn(UserBase):
    password: str

class UserOut(UserBase):
    pass

class UserInDB(UserBase):
    hashed_password: str

def fake_save_user(user_in: UserIn):
    hashed_password = fake_password_hasher(user_in.password)
    user_in_db = UserInDB(**user_in.model_dump(), hashed_password=hashed_password)
    return user_in_db

@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user_in: UserIn):
    return fake_save_user(user_in)
```

**`**user_in.model_dump()`:** `.model_dump()` → `dict` der Modelldaten; `**` entpackt ihn zu Keyword-Argumenten; zusätzliche Kwargs (`hashed_password=...`) lassen sich anhängen. `UserInDB(**user_in.model_dump(), hashed_password=hashed_password)`.

**Union / `anyOf`:** spezifischeren Typ zuerst.
```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem)
```
Als *Wert eines Arguments* ist in älterem Code `Union[PlaneItem, CarItem]` nötig — `response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem` funktioniert nur, weil Python 3.10+ `|` auf Klassen unterstützt; in einer echten Typ-Annotation ist `|` immer ok.

**Liste / Dict:**
```python
@app.get("/items/", response_model=list[Item])
@app.get("/keyword-weights/", response_model=dict[str, float])
```
`dict[str, float]` ist nützlich, wenn Feldnamen vorab unbekannt sind.

---

## 3. `response-status-code`

**Kernidee:** `status_code=` im Decorator setzt den Default-Statuscode der Response und dokumentiert ihn im OpenAPI-Schema.

```python
@app.post("/items/", status_code=201)
async def create_item(name: str): ...

from fastapi import FastAPI, status
@app.post("/items/", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
```
- Auch ein `IntEnum` (z. B. `http.HTTPStatus`) ist erlaubt.
- `fastapi.status` == `starlette.status` (nur Convenience, Autocomplete).

**Klassen:** 1xx Info (nie Body) · 2xx Success (`200` Default, `201` Created, **`204` No Content — darf keinen Body haben**) · 3xx Redirect (Body optional, **`304` Not Modified darf keinen Body haben**) · 4xx Client-Fehler (`404`, generisch `400`) · 5xx Server-Fehler (i. d. R. automatisch).
FastAPI weiß, welche Codes keinen Body haben, und dokumentiert das entsprechend in OpenAPI.

---

## 4. `request-forms`

**Kernidee:** Für HTML-Formulardaten statt JSON `Form()` verwenden; ohne `Form` würden die Parameter als Query- oder JSON-Body-Parameter interpretiert.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form

@app.post("/login/")
async def login(username: Annotated[str, Form()], password: Annotated[str, Form()]):
    return {"username": username}
```
- Braucht `uv add python-multipart` (Formdaten-Parser).
- `Form` erbt direkt von `Body` → gleiche Validierungen, `examples`, `alias` usw.
- Encoding: `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (ohne Dateien), `multipart/form-data` (mit Dateien).
- **Form und JSON-Body nicht mischbar:** mehrere `Form`-Parameter sind ok, aber keine zusätzlichen `Body`-Felder, weil der Body dann formkodiert statt `application/json` ist. Das ist eine HTTP-Einschränkung, keine von FastAPI.
- Typischer Anwendungsfall: OAuth2 Password Flow verlangt `username`/`password` als Formfelder.

---

## 5. `request-form-models` (ab FastAPI 0.113.0)

**Kernidee:** Ein Pydantic-Modell kann die Formfelder bündeln — Parameter mit `Form()` annotieren, FastAPI extrahiert jedes Feld aus den Formdaten.

```python
class FormData(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str

@app.post("/login/")
async def login(data: Annotated[FormData, Form()]):
    return data
```

**Extra-Felder verbieten (ab 0.114.0):**
```python
class FormData(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}
```
Ein Extra-Feld erzeugt `{"type": "extra_forbidden", "loc": ["body", "extra"], "msg": "Extra inputs are not permitted"}`.

---

## 6. `request-files`

**Kernidee:** `File()` deklariert Datei-Uploads (kommen als Formdaten). `bytes` liest die ganze Datei in den Speicher, `UploadFile` nutzt eine gespoolte Datei (Speicher bis Limit, danach Disk) und bietet Metadaten plus async-File-Interface.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, File, UploadFile

@app.post("/files/")
async def create_file(file: Annotated[bytes, File()]):
    return {"file_size": len(file)}

@app.post("/uploadfile/")
async def create_upload_file(file: UploadFile):     # kein File() nötig
    return {"filename": file.filename}
```

**`UploadFile` Attribute:** `filename` (str), `content_type` (str, MIME), `file` (`SpooledTemporaryFile`, echtes file-like Objekt für andere Libraries).
**Async-Methoden (alle `await`en):** `write(data)`, `read(size)`, `seek(offset)` (z. B. `await myfile.seek(0)` nach einem vollen `read()`), `close()`.
```python
contents = await myfile.read()      # in async def
contents = myfile.file.read()       # in normalem def
```
Intern laufen die File-Methoden in einem Threadpool. FastAPIs `UploadFile` erbt von Starlettes und ergänzt Pydantic-Kompatibilität. `File` erbt direkt von `Form`.

**Optional:**
```python
async def create_file(file: Annotated[bytes | None, File()] = None): ...
async def create_upload_file(file: UploadFile | None = None): ...
```
**Mit Metadaten:**
```python
file: Annotated[UploadFile, File(description="A file read as UploadFile")]
```
**Mehrere Dateien (ein Formfeld, `<input name="files" type="file" multiple>`):**
```python
async def create_files(files: Annotated[list[bytes], File()]): ...
async def create_upload_files(files: list[UploadFile]): ...
# mit Metadaten:
files: Annotated[list[UploadFile], File(description="Multiple files as UploadFile")]
```
Braucht `python-multipart`. Gleiche Warnung: `File`/`Form` nicht mit JSON-`Body` mischbar (`multipart/form-data` statt `application/json`).

---

## 7. `request-forms-and-files`

**Kernidee:** `File` und `Form` lassen sich in derselben Path Operation kombinieren; einzelne Dateien dürfen `bytes`, andere `UploadFile` sein.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, File, Form, UploadFile

@app.post("/files/")
async def create_file(
    file: Annotated[bytes, File()],
    fileb: Annotated[UploadFile, File()],
    token: Annotated[str, Form()],
):
    return {"file_size": len(file), "token": token,
            "fileb_content_type": fileb.content_type}
```
Wieder: kein JSON-`Body` daneben.

---

## 8. `handling-errors`

**Kernidee:** Fehler an den Client meldet man mit `raise HTTPException(...)` — als Exception, nicht als Return-Wert; sie bricht die Verarbeitung sofort ab, auch aus Hilfsfunktionen heraus.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    if item_id not in items:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return {"item": items[item_id]}
# -> 404, {"detail": "Item not found"}
```
`detail` darf alles JSON-fähige sein (`dict`, `list`, …), nicht nur `str`.

**Custom Header:**
```python
raise HTTPException(
    status_code=404,
    detail="Item not found",
    headers={"X-Error": "There goes my error"},
)
```

**Eigener Exception-Handler:**
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

class UnicornException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name

@app.exception_handler(UnicornException)
async def unicorn_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: UnicornException):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=418,
        content={"message": f"Oops! {exc.name} did something. There goes a rainbow..."},
    )
```

**Default-Handler überschreiben** (`RequestValidationError` = bei ungültigen Request-Daten intern geworfen; Handler bekommt `Request` + Exception):
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError
from fastapi.responses import PlainTextResponse
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException

@app.exception_handler(StarletteHTTPException)
async def http_exception_handler(request, exc):
    return PlainTextResponse(str(exc.detail), status_code=exc.status_code)

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    message = "Validation errors:"
    for error in exc.errors():
        message += f"\nField: {error['loc']}, Error: {error['msg']}"
    return PlainTextResponse(message, status_code=400)
```
Warnung: `RequestValidationError` enthält Dateiname/Zeile des Fehlers — nicht einfach `str(exc)` ausgeben (Info-Leak), sondern Felder einzeln extrahieren.

**`exc.body` nutzen:**
```python
@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=422,
        content=jsonable_encoder({"detail": exc.errors(), "body": exc.body}),
    )
```

**FastAPI- vs. Starlette-`HTTPException`:** FastAPIs erbt von Starlettes; einziger Unterschied — FastAPIs `detail` akzeptiert beliebige JSON-fähige Daten, Starlettes nur Strings. Im eigenen Code weiter FastAPIs `HTTPException` raisen, den **Handler aber für `StarletteHTTPException` registrieren**, damit auch von Starlette-internem Code / Plugins geworfene Exceptions erfasst werden.

**`RequestValidationError` vs. `ValidationError`:** `RequestValidationError` (FastAPI, Subklasse von Pydantics `ValidationError`) betrifft **eingehende Client-Daten** → 422. Ein Validierungsfehler in der *Response* ist ein Bug in deinem Code → Server-Fehler (500), nicht 422.

**Default-Handler wiederverwenden:**
```python
from fastapi.exception_handlers import (
    http_exception_handler,
    request_validation_exception_handler,
)

@app.exception_handler(StarletteHTTPException)
async def custom_http_exception_handler(request, exc):
    print(f"OMG! An HTTP error!: {repr(exc)}")
    return await http_exception_handler(request, exc)

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request, exc):
    print(f"OMG! The client sent invalid data!: {exc}")
    return await request_validation_exception_handler(request, exc)
```

---

## 9. `path-operation-configuration`

**Kernidee:** Metadaten werden als Parameter an den **Decorator** übergeben (nicht an die Funktion) und landen im OpenAPI-Schema / in der Docs-UI.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, status

@app.post("/items/", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item: ...
```

**Tags** (`list[str]`):
```python
@app.get("/items/", tags=["items"])
@app.get("/users/", tags=["users"])
```
**Tags als Enum** (bei großen Apps, um Tippfehler/Divergenz zu vermeiden):
```python
from enum import Enum

class Tags(Enum):
    items = "items"
    users = "users"

@app.get("/items/", tags=[Tags.items])
async def get_items(): ...
```

**summary / description:**
```python
@app.post(
    "/items/",
    summary="Create an item",
    description="Create an item with all the information, name, description, price, tax and a set of unique tags",
)
```
**description aus Docstring** (Markdown wird gerendert, Einrückung berücksichtigt):
```python
@app.post("/items/", summary="Create an item", response_description="The created item")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    """
    Create an item with all the information:

    - **name**: each item must have a name
    - **description**: a long description
    - **price**: required
    - **tax**: if the item doesn't have tax, you can omit this
    - **tags**: a set of unique tag strings for this item
    """
    return item
```
- `response_description` beschreibt speziell die **Response**, `description` die Path Operation insgesamt. OpenAPI verlangt eine Response-Beschreibung; ohne Angabe generiert FastAPI "Successful response".

**deprecated:**
```python
@app.get("/elements/", tags=["items"], deprecated=True)
async def read_elements(): ...
```

---

## 10. `encoder` — `jsonable_encoder`

**Kernidee:** `jsonable_encoder(obj)` konvertiert beliebige Objekte (Pydantic-Modell, `datetime`, …) in **JSON-kompatible Python-Datenstrukturen** (`dict`, `list`, `str`, …) — nicht in einen JSON-String. Ergebnis ist mit `json.dumps()` serialisierbar. Nötig, wenn man Daten in eine DB schreibt, die nur JSON-fähige Typen akzeptiert (z. B. NoSQL).

```python
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

@app.put("/items/{id}")
def update_item(id: str, item: Item):
    json_compatible_item_data = jsonable_encoder(item)   # Modell -> dict, datetime -> str
    fake_db[id] = json_compatible_item_data
```
FastAPI nutzt es intern selbst.

---

## 11. `body-updates` — PUT vs. PATCH

**Kernidee:** `PUT` **ersetzt** den Datensatz vollständig — nicht mitgeschickte Felder fallen auf die Modell-Defaults zurück (stiller Datenverlust). `PATCH` aktualisiert **partiell** über `exclude_unset` + `model_copy(update=...)`.

**PUT-Falle:** Body `{"name": "Barz", "price": 3, "description": None}` ohne `tax` → gespeichertes `"tax": 20.2` wird durch den Default `10.5` überschrieben.

**PATCH-Rezept (exakt):**
```python
@app.patch("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: str, item: Item) -> Item:
    stored_item_data = items[item_id]
    stored_item_model = Item(**stored_item_data)          # gespeicherte Daten ins Modell
    update_data = item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)     # nur wirklich gesendete Felder
    updated_item = stored_item_model.model_copy(update=update_data)
    items[item_id] = jsonable_encoder(updated_item)       # DB-taugliche Form
    return updated_item
```
Schritte: (optional) `PATCH` statt `PUT` → gespeicherte Daten holen → in Pydantic-Modell → `dict` ohne Defaults via `exclude_unset=True` → `model_copy(update=...)` auf der Kopie des gespeicherten Modells → `jsonable_encoder` (wie `.model_dump()`, konvertiert aber zusätzlich z. B. `datetime` → `str`) → speichern → aktualisiertes Modell zurückgeben.

**Wichtig:** Das Input-Modell wird weiterhin validiert. Damit wirklich alle Felder weggelassen werden dürfen, muss das Update-Modell alle Attribute optional haben (`str | None = None`) — daher getrennte Create-/Update-Modelle (siehe `extra-models`). Die Technik funktioniert genauso mit `PUT`; `PATCH` ist nur die semantisch dafür vorgesehene Methode und wird in der Praxis seltener genutzt.

toolCalls.result:
1	# Dependencies with yield { #dependencies-with-yield }
2	
3	FastAPI supports dependencies that do some <dfn title='sometimes also called "exit code", "cleanup code", "teardown code", "closing code", "context manager exit code", etc.'>extra steps after finishing</dfn>.
4	
5	To do this, use `yield` instead of `return`, and write the extra steps (code) after.
6	
7	/// tip
8	
9	Make sure to use `yield` one single time per dependency.
10	
11	///
12	
13	/// note | Technical Details
14	
15	Any function that is valid to use with:
16	
17	* [`@contextlib.contextmanager`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html#contextlib.contextmanager) or
18	* [`@contextlib.asynccontextmanager`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html#contextlib.asynccontextmanager)
19	
20	would be valid to use as a **FastAPI** dependency.
21	
22	In fact, FastAPI uses those two decorators internally.
23	
24	///
25	
26	## A database dependency with `yield` { #a-database-dependency-with-yield }
27	
28	For example, you could use this to create a database session and close it after finishing.
29	
30	Only the code prior to and including the `yield` statement is executed before creating a response:
31	
32	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial007_py310.py hl[2:4] *}
33	
34	The yielded value is what is injected into *path operations* and other dependencies:
35	
36	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial007_py310.py hl[4] *}
37	
38	The code following the `yield` statement is executed after the response:
39	
40	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial007_py310.py hl[5:6] *}
41	
42	/// tip
43	
44	You can use `async` or regular functions.
45	
46	**FastAPI** will do the right thing with each, the same as with normal dependencies.
47	
48	///
49	
50	## A dependency with `yield` and `try` { #a-dependency-with-yield-and-try }
51	
52	If you use a `try` block in a dependency with `yield`, you'll receive any exception that was thrown when using the dependency.
53	
54	For example, if some code at some point in the middle, in another dependency or in a *path operation*, made a database transaction "rollback" or created any other exception, you would receive the exception in your dependency.
55	
56	So, you can look for that specific exception inside the dependency with `except SomeException`.
57	
58	In the same way, you can use `finally` to make sure the exit steps are executed, no matter if there was an exception or not.
59	
60	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial007_py310.py hl[3,5] *}
61	
62	## Sub-dependencies with `yield` { #sub-dependencies-with-yield }
63	
64	You can have sub-dependencies and "trees" of sub-dependencies of any size and shape, and any or all of them can use `yield`.
65	
66	**FastAPI** will make sure that the "exit code" in each dependency with `yield` is run in the correct order.
67	
68	For example, `dependency_c` can have a dependency on `dependency_b`, and `dependency_b` on `dependency_a`:
69	
70	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008_an_py310.py hl[6,14,22] *}
71	
72	And all of them can use `yield`.
73	
74	In this case `dependency_c`, to execute its exit code, needs the value from `dependency_b` (here named `dep_b`) to still be available.
75	
76	And, in turn, `dependency_b` needs the value from `dependency_a` (here named `dep_a`) to be available for its exit code.
77	
78	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008_an_py310.py hl[18:19,26:27] *}
79	
80	The same way, you could have some dependencies with `yield` and some other dependencies with `return`, and have some of those depend on some of the others.
81	
82	And you could have a single dependency that requires several other dependencies with `yield`, etc.
83	
84	You can have any combinations of dependencies that you want.
85	
86	**FastAPI** will make sure everything is run in the correct order.
87	
88	/// note | Technical Details
89	
90	This works thanks to Python's [Context Managers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html).
91	
92	**FastAPI** uses them internally to achieve this.
93	
94	///
95	
96	## Dependencies with `yield` and `HTTPException` { #dependencies-with-yield-and-httpexception }
97	
98	You saw that you can use dependencies with `yield` and have `try` blocks that try to execute some code and then run some exit code after `finally`.
99	
100	You can also use `except` to catch the exception that was raised and do something with it.
101	
102	For example, you can raise a different exception, like `HTTPException`.
103	
104	/// tip
105	
106	This is a somewhat advanced technique, and in most of the cases you won't really need it, as you can raise exceptions (including `HTTPException`) from inside of the rest of your application code, for example, in the *path operation function*.
107	
108	But it's there for you if you need it. 🤓
109	
110	///
111	
112	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008b_an_py310.py hl[18:22,31] *}
113	
114	If you want to catch exceptions and create a custom response based on that, create a [Custom Exception Handler](../handling-errors.md#install-custom-exception-handlers).
115	
116	## Dependencies with `yield` and `except` { #dependencies-with-yield-and-except }
117	
118	If you catch an exception using `except` in a dependency with `yield` and you don't raise it again (or raise a new exception), FastAPI won't be able to notice there was an exception, the same way that would happen with regular Python:
119	
120	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008c_an_py310.py hl[15:16] *}
121	
122	In this case, the client will see an *HTTP 500 Internal Server Error* response as it should, given that we are not raising an `HTTPException` or similar, but the server will **not have any logs** or any other indication of what was the error. 😱
123	
124	### Always `raise` in Dependencies with `yield` and `except` { #always-raise-in-dependencies-with-yield-and-except }
125	
126	If you catch an exception in a dependency with `yield`, unless you are raising another `HTTPException` or similar, **you should re-raise the original exception**.
127	
128	You can re-raise the same exception using `raise`:
129	
130	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008d_an_py310.py hl[17] *}
131	
132	Now the client will get the same *HTTP 500 Internal Server Error* response, but the server will have our custom `InternalError` in the logs. 😎
133	
134	## Execution of dependencies with `yield` { #execution-of-dependencies-with-yield }
135	
136	The sequence of execution is more or less like this diagram. Time flows from top to bottom. And each column is one of the parts interacting or executing code.
137	
138	```mermaid
139	sequenceDiagram
140	
141	participant client as Client
142	participant handler as Exception handler
143	participant dep as Dep with yield
144	participant operation as Path Operation
145	participant tasks as Background tasks
146	
147	    Note over client,operation: Can raise exceptions, including HTTPException
148	    client ->> dep: Start request
149	    Note over dep: Run code up to yield
150	    opt raise Exception
151	        dep -->> handler: Raise Exception
152	        handler -->> client: HTTP error response
153	    end
154	    dep ->> operation: Run dependency, e.g. DB session
155	    opt raise
156	        operation -->> dep: Raise Exception (e.g. HTTPException)
157	        opt handle
158	            dep -->> dep: Can catch exception, raise a new HTTPException, raise other exception
159	        end
160	        handler -->> client: HTTP error response
161	    end
162	
163	    operation ->> client: Return response to client
164	    Note over client,operation: Response is already sent, can't change it anymore
165	    opt Tasks
166	        operation -->> tasks: Send background tasks
167	    end
168	    opt Raise other exception
169	        tasks -->> tasks: Handle exceptions in the background task code
170	    end
171	```
172	
173	/// note
174	
175	Only **one response** will be sent to the client. It might be one of the error responses or it will be the response from the *path operation*.
176	
177	After one of those responses is sent, no other response can be sent.
178	
179	///
180	
181	/// tip
182	
183	If you raise any exception in the code from the *path operation function*, it will be passed to the dependencies with yield, including `HTTPException`. In most cases you will want to re-raise that same exception or a new one from the dependency with `yield` to make sure it's properly handled.
184	
185	///
186	
187	## Early exit and `scope` { #early-exit-and-scope }
188	
189	Normally the exit code of dependencies with `yield` is executed **after the response** is sent to the client.
190	
191	But if you know that you won't need to use the dependency after returning from the *path operation function*, you can use `Depends(scope="function")` to tell FastAPI that it should close the dependency after the *path operation function* returns, but **before** the **response is sent**.
192	
193	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial008e_an_py310.py hl[12,16] *}
194	
195	`Depends()` receives a `scope` parameter that can be:
196	
197	* `"function"`: start the dependency before the *path operation function* that handles the request, end the dependency after the *path operation function* ends, but **before** the response is sent back to the client. So, the dependency function will be executed **around** the *path operation **function***.
198	* `"request"`: start the dependency before the *path operation function* that handles the request (similar to when using `"function"`), but end **after** the response is sent back to the client. So, the dependency function will be executed **around** the **request** and response cycle.
199	
200	If not specified and the dependency has `yield`, it will have a `scope` of `"request"` by default.
201	
202	### `scope` for sub-dependencies { #scope-for-sub-dependencies }
203	
204	When you declare a dependency with a `scope="request"` (the default), any sub-dependency needs to also have a `scope` of `"request"`.
205	
206	But a dependency with `scope` of `"function"` can have dependencies with `scope` of `"function"` and `scope` of `"request"`.
207	
208	This is because any dependency needs to be able to run its exit code before the sub-dependencies, as it might need to still use them during its exit code.
209	
210	```mermaid
211	sequenceDiagram
212	
213	participant client as Client
214	participant dep_req as Dep scope="request"
215	participant dep_func as Dep scope="function"
216	participant operation as Path Operation
217	
218	    client ->> dep_req: Start request
219	    Note over dep_req: Run code up to yield
220	    dep_req ->> dep_func: Pass dependency
221	    Note over dep_func: Run code up to yield
222	    dep_func ->> operation: Run path operation with dependency
223	    operation ->> dep_func: Return from path operation
224	    Note over dep_func: Run code after yield
225	    Note over dep_func: ✅ Dependency closed
226	    dep_func ->> client: Send response to client
227	    Note over client: Response sent
228	    Note over dep_req: Run code after yield
229	    Note over dep_req: ✅ Dependency closed
230	```
231	
232	## Dependencies with `yield`, `HTTPException`, `except` and Background Tasks { #dependencies-with-yield-httpexception-except-and-background-tasks }
233	
234	Dependencies with `yield` have evolved over time to cover different use cases and fix some issues.
235	
236	If you want to see what has changed in different versions of FastAPI, you can read more about it in the advanced guide, in [Advanced Dependencies - Dependencies with `yield`, `HTTPException`, `except` and Background Tasks](../../advanced/advanced-dependencies.md#dependencies-with-yield-httpexception-except-and-background-tasks).
237	
238	## Context Managers { #context-managers }
239	
240	### What are "Context Managers" { #what-are-context-managers }
241	
242	"Context Managers" are any of those Python objects that you can use in a `with` statement.
243	
244	For example, [you can use `with` to read a file](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#reading-and-writing-files):
245	
246	```Python
247	with open("./somefile.txt") as f:
248	    contents = f.read()
249	    print(contents)
250	```
251	
252	Underneath, the `open("./somefile.txt")` creates an object that is called a "Context Manager".
253	
254	When the `with` block finishes, it makes sure to close the file, even if there were exceptions.
255	
256	When you create a dependency with `yield`, **FastAPI** will internally create a context manager for it, and combine it with some other related tools.
257	
258	### Using context managers in dependencies with `yield` { #using-context-managers-in-dependencies-with-yield }
259	
260	/// warning
261	
262	This is, more or less, an "advanced" idea.
263	
264	If you are just starting with **FastAPI** you might want to skip it for now.
265	
266	///
267	
268	In Python, you can create Context Managers by [creating a class with two methods: `__enter__()` and `__exit__()`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#context-managers).
269	
270	You can also use them inside of **FastAPI** dependencies with `yield` by using
271	`with` or `async with` statements inside of the dependency function:

277	Another way to create a context manager is with:

280	* [`@contextlib.asynccontextmanager`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html#contextlib.asynccontextmanager)

283

toolCalls.result: 1 # Dependencies { #dependencies } 2 3 **FastAPI** has a very powerful but intuitive **Dependency Injection** system. 4 5 It is designed to be very simple to use, and to make it very easy for any developer to integrate other components with **FastAPI**. 6 7 ## What is "Dependency Injection" { #what-is-dependency-injection } 8 9 **"Dependency Injection"** means, in programming, that there is a way for your code (in this case, your *path operation functions*) to declare things that it requires to work and use: "dependencies". 10 11 And then, that system (in this case **FastAPI**) will take care of doing whatever is needed to provide your code with those needed dependencies ("inject" the dependencies). 12 13 This is very useful when you need to: 14 15 * Have shared logic (the same code logic again and again). 16 * Share database connections. 17 * Enforce security, authentication, role requirements, etc. 18 * And many other things... 19 20 All these, while minimizing code repetition. 21 22 ## First Steps { #first-steps } 23 24 Let's see a very simple example. It will be so simple that it is not very useful, for now. 25 26 But this way we can focus on how the **Dependency Injection** system works. 27 28 ### Create a dependency, or "dependable" { #create-a-dependency-or-dependable } 29 30 Let's first focus on the dependency. 31 32 It is just a function that can take all the same parameters that a *path operation function* can take: 33 34 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[8:9] *} 35 36 That's it. 37 38 **2 lines**. 39 40 And it has the same shape and structure that all your *path operation functions* have. 41 42 You can think of it as a *path operation function* without the "decorator" (without the `@app.get("/some-path")`). 43 44 And it can return anything you want. 45 46 In this case, this dependency expects: 47 48 * An optional query parameter `q` that is a `str`. 49 * An optional query parameter `skip` that is an `int`, and by default is `0`. 50 * An optional query parameter `limit` that is an `int`, and by default is `100`. 51 52 And then it just returns a `dict` containing those values. 53 54 /// note 55 56 FastAPI added support for `Annotated` (and started recommending it) in version 0.95.0. 57 58 If you have an older version, you would get errors when trying to use `Annotated`. 59 60 Make sure you [Upgrade the FastAPI version](../../deployment/versions.md#upgrading-the-fastapi-versions) to at least 0.95.1 before using `Annotated`. 61 62 /// 63 64 ### Import `Depends` { #import-depends } 65 66 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[3] *} 67 68 ### Declare the dependency, in the "dependant" { #declare-the-dependency-in-the-dependant } 69 70 The same way you use `Body`, `Query`, etc. with your *path operation function* parameters, use `Depends` with a new parameter: 71 72 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[13,18] *} 73 74 Although you use `Depends` in the parameters of your function the same way you use `Body`, `Query`, etc, `Depends` works a bit differently. 75 76 You only give `Depends` a single parameter. 77 78 This parameter must be something like a function. 79 80 You **don't call it** directly (don't add the parenthesis at the end), you just pass it as a parameter to `Depends()`. 81 82 And that function takes parameters in the same way that *path operation functions* do. 83 84 /// tip 85 86 You'll see what other "things", apart from functions, can be used as dependencies in the next chapter. 87 88 /// 89 90 Whenever a new request arrives, **FastAPI** will take care of: 91 92 * Calling your dependency ("dependable") function with the correct parameters. 93 * Get the result from your function. 94 * Assign that result to the parameter in your *path operation function*. 95 96 ```mermaid 97 graph TB 98 99 common_parameters(["common_parameters"]) 100 read_items["/items/"] 101 read_users["/users/"] 102 103 common_parameters --> read_items 104 common_parameters --> read_users 105 ``` 106 107 This way you write shared code once and **FastAPI** takes care of calling it for your *path operations*. 108 109 /// tip 110 111 Notice that you don't have to create a special class and pass it somewhere to **FastAPI** to "register" it or anything similar. 112 113 You just pass it to `Depends` and **FastAPI** knows how to do the rest. 114 115 /// 116 117 ## Share `Annotated` dependencies { #share-annotated-dependencies } 118 119 In the examples above, you see that there's a tiny bit of **code duplication**. 120 121 When you need to use the `common_parameters()` dependency, you have to write the whole parameter with the type annotation and `Depends()`: 122 123 ```Python 124 commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)] 125 ``` 126 127 But because we are using `Annotated`, we can store that `Annotated` value in a variable and use it in multiple places: 128 129 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial001_02_an_py310.py hl[12,16,21] *} 130 131 /// tip 132 133 This is just standard Python, it's called a "type alias", it's actually not specific to **FastAPI**. 134 135 But because **FastAPI** is based on the Python standards, including `Annotated`, you can use this trick in your code. 😎 136 137 /// 138 139 The dependencies will keep working as expected, and the **best part** is that the **type information will be preserved**, which means that your editor will be able to keep providing you with **autocompletion**, **inline errors**, etc. The same for other tools like `mypy`. 140 141 This will be especially useful when you use it in a **large code base** where you use **the same dependencies** over and over again in **many *path operations***. 142 143 ## To `async` or not to `async` { #to-async-or-not-to-async } 144 145 As dependencies will also be called by **FastAPI** (the same as your *path operation functions*), the same rules apply while defining your functions. 146 147 You can use `async def` or normal `def`. 148 149 And you can declare dependencies with `async def` inside of normal `def` *path operation functions*, or `def` dependencies inside of `async def` *path operation functions*, etc. 150 151 It doesn't matter. **FastAPI** will know what to do. 152 153 /// note 154 155 If you don't know, check the [Async: *"In a hurry?"*](../../async.md#in-a-hurry) section about `async` and `await` in the docs. 156 157 /// 158 159 ## Integrated with OpenAPI { #integrated-with-openapi } 160 161 All the request declarations, validations and requirements of your dependencies (and sub-dependencies) will be integrated in the same OpenAPI schema. 162 163 So, the interactive docs will have all the information from these dependencies too: 164 165 166 167 ## Simple usage { #simple-usage } 168 169 If you look at it, *path operation functions* are declared to be used whenever a *path* and *operation* matches, and then **FastAPI** takes care of calling the function with the correct parameters, extracting the data from the request. 170 171 Actually, all (or most) of the web frameworks work in this same way. 172 173 You never call those functions directly. They are called by your framework (in this case, **FastAPI**). 174 175 With the Dependency Injection system, you can also tell **FastAPI** that your *path operation function* also "depends" on something else that should be executed before your *path operation function*, and **FastAPI** will take care of executing it and "injecting" the results. 176 177 Other common terms for this same idea of "dependency injection" are: 178 179 * resources 180 * providers 181 * services 182 * injectables 183 * components 184 185 ## **FastAPI** plug-ins { #fastapi-plug-ins } 186 187 Integrations and "plug-ins" can be built using the **Dependency Injection** system. But in fact, there is actually **no need to create "plug-ins"**, as by using dependencies it's possible to declare an infinite number of integrations and interactions that become available to your *path operation functions*. 188 189 And dependencies can be created in a very simple and intuitive way that allows you to just import the Python packages you need, and integrate them with your API functions in a couple of lines of code, *literally*. 190 191 You will see examples of this in the next chapters, about relational and NoSQL databases, security, etc. 192 193 ## **FastAPI** compatibility { #fastapi-compatibility } 194 195 The simplicity of the dependency injection system makes **FastAPI** compatible with: 196 197 * all the relational databases 198 * NoSQL databases 199 * external packages 200 * external APIs 201 * authentication and authorization systems 202 * API usage monitoring systems 203 * response data injection systems 204 * etc. 205 206 ## Simple and Powerful { #simple-and-powerful } 207 208 Although the hierarchical dependency injection system is very simple to define and use, it's still very powerful. 209 210 You can define dependencies that in turn can define dependencies themselves. 211 212 In the end, a hierarchical tree of dependencies is built, and the **Dependency Injection** system takes care of solving all these dependencies for you (and their sub-dependencies) and providing (injecting) the results at each step. 213 214 For example, let's say you have 4 API endpoints (*path operations*): 215 216 * `/items/public/` 217 * `/items/private/` 218 * `/users/{user_id}/activate` 219 * `/items/pro/` 220 221 then you could add different permission requirements for each of them just with dependencies and sub-dependencies: 222 223 ```mermaid 224 graph TB 225 226 current_user(["current_user"]) 227 active_user(["active_user"]) 228 admin_user(["admin_user"]) 229 paying_user(["paying_user"]) 230 231 public["/items/public/"] 232 private["/items/private/"] 233 activate_user["/users/{user_id}/activate"] 234 pro_items["/items/pro/"] 235 236 current_user --> active_user 237 active_user --> admin_user 238 active_user --> paying_user 239 240 current_user --> public 241 active_user --> private 242 admin_user --> activate_user 243 paying_user --> pro_items 244 ``` 245 246 ## Integrated with **OpenAPI** { #integrated-with-openapi_1 } 247 248 All these dependencies, while declaring their requirements, also add parameters, validations, etc. to your *path operations*. 249 250 **FastAPI** will take care of adding it all to the OpenAPI schema, so that it is shown in the interactive documentation systems. 251

1	# Sub-dependencies { #sub-dependencies }
2	
3	You can create dependencies that have **sub-dependencies**.
4	
5	They can be as **deep** as you need them to be.
6	
7	**FastAPI** will take care of solving them.
8	
9	## First dependency "dependable" { #first-dependency-dependable }
10	
11	You could create a first dependency ("dependable") like:
12	
13	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[8:9] *}
14	
15	It declares an optional query parameter `q` as a `str`, and then it just returns it.
16	
17	This is quite simple (not very useful), but will help us focus on how the sub-dependencies work.
18	
19	## Second dependency, "dependable" and "dependant" { #second-dependency-dependable-and-dependant }
20	
21	Then you can create another dependency function (a "dependable") that at the same time declares a dependency of its own (so it is a "dependant" too):
22	
23	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[13] *}
24	
25	Let's focus on the parameters declared:
26	
27	* Even though this function is a dependency ("dependable") itself, it also declares another dependency (it "depends" on something else).
28	    * It depends on the `query_extractor`, and assigns the value returned by it to the parameter `q`.
29	* It also declares an optional `last_query` cookie, as a `str`.
30	    * If the user didn't provide any query `q`, we use the last query used, which we saved to a cookie before.
31	
32	## Use the dependency { #use-the-dependency }
33	
34	Then we can use the dependency with:
35	
36	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[23] *}
37	
38	/// note
39	
40	Notice that we are only declaring one dependency in the *path operation function*, the `query_or_cookie_extractor`.
41	
42	But **FastAPI** will know that it has to solve `query_extractor` first, to pass the results of that to `query_or_cookie_extractor` while calling it.
43	
44	///
45	
46	```mermaid
47	graph TB
48	
49	query_extractor(["query_extractor"])
50	query_or_cookie_extractor(["query_or_cookie_extractor"])
51	
52	read_query["/items/"]
53	
54	query_extractor --> query_or_cookie_extractor --> read_query
55	```
56	
57	## Using the same dependency multiple times { #using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times }
58	
59	If one of your dependencies is declared multiple times for the same *path operation*, for example, multiple dependencies have a common sub-dependency, **FastAPI** will know to call that sub-dependency only once per request.
60	
61	And it will save the returned value in a <dfn title="A utility/system to store computed/generated values, to reuse them instead of computing them again.">"cache"</dfn> and pass it to all the "dependants" that need it in that specific request, instead of calling the dependency multiple times for the same request.
62	
63	In an advanced scenario where you know you need the dependency to be called at every step (possibly multiple times) in the same request instead of using the "cached" value, you can set the parameter `use_cache=False` when using `Depends`:
64	
65	//// tab | Python 3.10+
66	
67	```Python hl_lines="1"
68	async def needy_dependency(fresh_value: Annotated[str, Depends(get_value, use_cache=False)]):
69	    return {"fresh_value": fresh_value}
70	```
71	
72	////
73	
74	//// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated
75	
76	/// tip
77	
78	Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible.
79	
80	///
81	
82	```Python hl_lines="1"
83	async def needy_dependency(fresh_value: str = Depends(get_value, use_cache=False)):
84	    return {"fresh_value": fresh_value}
85	```
86	
87	////
88	
89	## Recap { #recap }
90	
91	Apart from all the fancy words used here, the **Dependency Injection** system is quite simple.
92	
93	Just functions that look the same as the *path operation functions*.
94	
95	But still, it is very powerful, and allows you to declare arbitrarily deeply nested dependency "graphs" (trees).
96	
97	/// tip
98	
99	All this might not seem as useful with these simple examples.
100	
101	But you will see how useful it is in the chapters about **security**.
102	
103	And you will also see the amounts of code it will save you.
104	
105	///
106

What makes a dependency { #what-makes-a-dependency } 18 19 Up to now you have seen dependencies declared as functions. 20 21 But that's not the only way to declare dependencies (although it would probably be the more common). 22 23 The key factor is that a dependency should be a "callable". 24 25 A "**callable**" in Python is anything that Python can "call" like a function. 26 27 So, if you have an object `something` (that might _not_ be a function) and you can "call" it (execute it) like: 28 29 ```Python 30 something() 31 ``` 32 33 or 34 35 ```Python 36 something(some_argument, some_keyword_argument="foo") 37 ``` 38 39 then it is a "callable". 40 41 ## Classes as dependencies { #classes-as-dependencies_1 } 42 43 You might notice that to create an instance of a Python class, you use that same syntax. 44 45 For example: 46 47 ```Python 48 class Cat: 49 def __init__(self, name: str): 50 self.name = name 51 52 53 fluffy = Cat(name="Mr Fluffy") 54 ``` 55 56 In this case, `fluffy` is an instance of the class `Cat`. 57 58 And to create `fluffy`, you are "calling" `Cat`. 59 60 So, a Python class is also a **callable**. 61 62 Then, in **FastAPI**, you could use a Python class as a dependency. 63 64 What FastAPI actually checks is that it is a "callable" (function, class or anything else) and the parameters defined. 65 66 If you pass a "callable" as a dependency in **FastAPI**, it will analyze the parameters for that "callable", and process them in the same way as the parameters for a *path operation function*. Including sub-dependencies. 67 68 That also applies to callables with no parameters at all. The same as it would be for *path operation functions* with no parameters. 69 70 Then, we can change the dependency "dependable" `common_parameters` from above to the class `CommonQueryParams`: 71 72 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[11:15] *} 73 74 Pay attention to the `__init__` method used to create the instance of the class: 75 76 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[12] *} 77 78 ...it has the same parameters as our previous `common_parameters`: 79 80 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[8] *} 81 82 Those parameters are what **FastAPI** will use to "solve" the dependency. 83 84 In both cases, it will have: 85 86 * An optional `q` query parameter that is a `str`. 87 * A `skip` query parameter that is an `int`, with a default of `0`. 88 * A `limit` query parameter that is an `int`, with a default of `100`. 89 90 In both cases the data will be converted, validated, documented on the OpenAPI schema, etc. 91 92 ## Use it { #use-it } 93 94 Now you can declare your dependency using this class. 95 96 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[19] *} 97 98 **FastAPI** calls the `CommonQueryParams` class. This creates an "instance" of that class and the instance will be passed as the parameter `commons` to your function. 99 100 ## Type annotation vs `Depends` { #type-annotation-vs-depends } 101 102 Notice how we write `CommonQueryParams` twice in the above code: 103 104 //// tab | Python 3.10+ 105 106 ```Python 107 commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends(CommonQueryParams)] 108 ``` 109 110 //// 111 112 //// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated 113 114 /// tip 115 116 Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. 117 118 /// 119 120 ```Python 121 commons: CommonQueryParams = Depends(CommonQueryParams) 122 ``` 123 124 //// 125 126 The last `CommonQueryParams`, in: 127 128 ```Python 129 ... Depends(CommonQueryParams) 130 ``` 131 132 ...is what **FastAPI** will actually use to know what is the dependency. 133 134 It is from this one that FastAPI will extract the declared parameters and that is what FastAPI will actually call. 135 136 --- 137 138 In this case, the first `CommonQueryParams`, in: 139 140 //// tab | Python 3.10+ 141 142 ```Python 143 commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, ... 144 ``` 145 146 //// 147 148 //// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated 149 150 /// tip 151 152 Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. 153 154 /// 155 156 ```Python 157 commons: CommonQueryParams ... 158 ``` 159 160 //// 161 162 ...doesn't have any special meaning for **FastAPI**. FastAPI won't use it for data conversion, validation, etc. (as it is using the `Depends(CommonQueryParams)` for that). 163 164 You could actually write just: 165 166 //// tab | Python 3.10+ 167 168 ```Python 169 commons: Annotated[Any, Depends(CommonQueryParams)] 170 ``` 171 172 //// 173 174 //// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated 175 176 /// tip 177 178 Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. 179 180 /// 181 182 ```Python 183 commons = Depends(CommonQueryParams) 184 ``` 185 186 //// 187 188 ...as in: 189 190 {* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[19] *} 191 192 But declaring the type is encouraged as that way your editor will know what will be passed as the parameter `commons`, and then it can help you with code completion, type checks, etc: 193 194 195 196 ## Shortcut { #shortcut } 197 198 But you see that we are having some code repetition here, writing `CommonQueryParams` twice: 199 200 //// tab | Python 3.10+ 201 202 ```Python 203 commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends(CommonQueryParams)] 204 ``` 205 206 //// 207 208 //// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated 209 210 /// tip 211 212 Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. 213 214 /// 215 216 ```Python 217 commons: CommonQueryParams = Depends(CommonQueryParams) 218 ``` 219 220 //// 221 222 **FastAPI** provides a shortcut for these cases, in where the dependency is *specifically* a class that **FastAPI** will "call" to create an instance of the class itself. 223 224 For those specific cases, you can do the following: 225 226 Instead of writing: 227 228 //// tab Python 3.10+ 253 254 ```Python 255 commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends()] 256 ``` 257 258 //// 259 260 //// tab | Python 3.10+ non-Annotated 261 262 /// tip 263 264 Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. 265 266 /// 267 268 ```Python 269 commons: CommonQueryParams = Depends() 270 ``` 271 272 //// 273 274 You declare the dependency as the type of the parameter, and you use `Depends()` without any parameter, instead of having to write the full class *again* inside of `Depends(CommonQueryParams)`. 275 276 The same example would then look like: 277 278 {* 1	# Dependencies in path operation decorators { #dependencies-in-path-operation-decorators }
2	
3	In some cases you don't really need the return value of a dependency inside your *path operation function*.
4	
5	Or the dependency doesn't return a value.
6	
7	But you still need it to be executed/solved.
8	
9	For those cases, instead of declaring a *path operation function* parameter with `Depends`, you can add a `list` of `dependencies` to the *path operation decorator*.
10	
11	## Add `dependencies` to the *path operation decorator* { #add-dependencies-to-the-path-operation-decorator }
12	
13	The *path operation decorator* receives an optional argument `dependencies`.
14	
15	It should be a `list` of `Depends()`:
16	
17	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[19] *}
18	
19	These dependencies will be executed/solved the same way as normal dependencies. But their value (if they return any) won't be passed to your *path operation function*.
20	
21	/// tip
22	
23	Some editors check for unused function parameters, and show them as errors.
24	
25	Using these `dependencies` in the *path operation decorator* you can make sure they are executed while avoiding editor/tooling errors.
26	
27	It might also help avoid confusion for new developers that see an unused parameter in your code and could think it's unnecessary.
28	
29	///
30	
31	/// note
32	
33	In this example we use invented custom headers `X-Key` and `X-Token`.
34	
35	But in real cases, when implementing security, you would get more benefits from using the integrated [Security utilities (the next chapter)](../security/index.md).
36	
37	///
38	
39	## Dependencies errors and return values { #dependencies-errors-and-return-values }
40	
41	You can use the same dependency *functions* you use normally.
42	
43	### Dependency requirements { #dependency-requirements }
44	
45	They can declare request requirements (like headers) or other sub-dependencies:
46	
47	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[8,13] *}

51	These dependencies can `raise` exceptions, the same as normal dependencies:
52	
53	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[10,15] *}

55	### Return values { #return-values }
56	
57	And they can return values or not, the values won't be used.
58	
59	So, you can reuse a normal dependency (that returns a value) you already use somewhere else, and even though the value won't be used, the dependency will be executed:
60	
61	{* ../../docs_src/dependencies/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[11,16] *}
62	
63	## Dependencies for a group of *path operations* { #dependencies-for-a-group-of-path-operations }

65	Later, when reading about how to structure bigger applications ([Bigger Applications - Multiple Files](../../tutorial/bigger-applications.md)), possibly with multiple files, you will learn how to declare a single `dependencies` parameter for a group of *path operations*.

1 # Security - First Steps { #security-first-steps } 2 3 Let's imagine that you have your **backend** API in some domain. 4 5 And you have a **frontend** in another domain or in a different path of the same domain (or in a mobile application). 6 7 And you want to have a way for the frontend to authenticate with the backend, using a **username** and **password**. 8 9 We can use **OAuth2** to build that with **FastAPI**. 10 11 But let's save you the time of reading the full long specification just to find those little pieces of information you need. 12 13 Let's use the tools provided by **FastAPI** to handle security. 14 15 ## How it looks { #how-it-looks } 16 17 Let's first just use the code and see how it works, and then we'll come back to understand what's happening. 18 19 ## Create `main.py` { #create-main-py } 20 21 Copy the example in a file `main.py`: 22 23 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial001_an_py310.py *} 24 25 ## Run it { #run-it } 26 27 /// note 28 29 The [`python-multipart`](https://github.com/Kludex/python-multipart) package is automatically installed with **FastAPI** when you run the `uv add "fastapi[standard]"` command. 30 31 However, if you use the `uv add fastapi` command, the `python-multipart` package is not included by default. 32 33 To install it manually, add it to your project with: 34 35 ```console 36 $ uv add python-multipart 37 ``` 38 39 This is because **OAuth2** uses "form data" for sending the `username` and `password`. 40 41 /// 42 43 Run the example with: 44 45
46 47 ```console 48 $ uv run fastapi dev 49 50 INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit) 51 ``` 52 53
54 55 ## Check it { #check-it } 56 57 Go to the interactive docs at: [http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs](http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs). 58 59 You will see something like this: 60 61 62 63 /// tip | Authorize button! 64 65 You already have a shiny new "Authorize" button. 66 67 And your *path operation* has a little lock in the top-right corner that you can click. 68 69 /// 70 71 And if you click it, you have a little authorization form to type a `username` and `password` (and other optional fields): 72 73 74 75 /// note 76 77 It doesn't matter what you type in the form, it won't work yet. But we'll get there. 78 79 /// 80 81 This is of course not the frontend for the final users, but it's a great automatic tool to document interactively all your API. 82 83 It can be used by the frontend team (that can also be yourself). 84 85 It can be used by third party applications and systems. 86 87 And it can also be used by yourself, to debug, check and test the same application. 88 89 ## The `password` flow { #the-password-flow } 90 91 Now let's go back a bit and understand what all that is. 92 93 The `password` "flow" is one of the ways ("flows") defined in OAuth2, to handle security and authentication. 94 95 OAuth2 was designed so that the backend or API could be independent of the server that authenticates the user. 96 97 But in this case, the same **FastAPI** application will handle the API and the authentication. 98 99 So, let's review it from that simplified point of view: 100 101 * The user types the `username` and `password` in the frontend, and hits `Enter`. 102 * The frontend (running in the user's browser) sends that `username` and `password` to a specific URL in our API (declared with `tokenUrl="token"`). 103 * The API checks that `username` and `password`, and responds with a "token" (we haven't implemented any of this yet). 104 * A "token" is just a string with some content that we can use later to verify this user. 105 * Normally, a token is set to expire after some time. 106 * So, the user will have to log in again at some point later. 107 * And if the token is stolen, the risk is less. It is not like a permanent key that will work forever (in most of the cases). 108 * The frontend stores that token temporarily somewhere. 109 * The user clicks in the frontend to go to another section of the frontend web app. 110 * The frontend needs to fetch some more data from the API. 111 * But it needs authentication for that specific endpoint. 112 * So, to authenticate with our API, it sends a header `Authorization` with a value of `Bearer ` plus the token. 113 * If the token contains `foobar`, the content of the `Authorization` header would be: `Bearer foobar`. 114 115 ## **FastAPI**'s `OAuth2PasswordBearer` { #fastapis-oauth2passwordbearer } 116 117 **FastAPI** provides several tools, at different levels of abstraction, to implement these security features. 118 119 In this example we are going to use **OAuth2**, with the **Password** flow, using a **Bearer** token. We do that using the `OAuth2PasswordBearer` class. 120 121 /// note 122 123 A "bearer" token is not the only option. 124 125 But it's the best one for our use case. 126 127 And it might be the best for most use cases, unless you are an OAuth2 expert and know exactly why there's another option that better suits your needs. 128 129 In that case, **FastAPI** also provides you with the tools to build it. 130 131 /// 132 133 When we create an instance of the `OAuth2PasswordBearer` class we pass in the `tokenUrl` parameter. This parameter contains the URL that the client (the frontend running in the user's browser) will use to send the `username` and `password` in order to get a token. 134 135 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[8] *} 136 137 /// tip 138 139 Here `tokenUrl="token"` refers to a relative URL `token` that we haven't created yet. As it's a relative URL, it's equivalent to `./token`. 140 141 Because we are using a relative URL, if your API was located at `https://example.com/`, then it would refer to `https://example.com/token`. But if your API was located at `https://example.com/api/v1/`, then it would refer to `https://example.com/api/v1/token`. 142 143 Using a relative URL is important to make sure your application keeps working even in an advanced use case like [Behind a Proxy](../../advanced/behind-a-proxy.md). 144 145 /// 146 147 This parameter doesn't create that endpoint / *path operation*, but declares that the URL `/token` will be the one that the client should use to get the token. That information is used in OpenAPI, and then in the interactive API documentation systems. 148 149 We will soon also create the actual path operation. 150 151 /// note 152 153 If you are a very strict "Pythonista" you might dislike the style of the parameter name `tokenUrl` instead of `token_url`. 154 155 That's because it is using the same name as in the OpenAPI spec. So that if you need to investigate more about any of these security schemes you can just copy and paste it to find more information about it. 156 157 /// 158 159 The `oauth2_scheme` variable is an instance of `OAuth2PasswordBearer`, but it is also a "callable". 160 161 It could be called as: 162 163 ```Python 164 oauth2_scheme(some, parameters) 165 ``` 166 167 So, it can be used with `Depends`. 168 169 ### Use it { #use-it } 170 171 Now you can pass that `oauth2_scheme` in a dependency with `Depends`. 172 173 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[12] *} 174 175 This dependency will provide a `str` that is assigned to the parameter `token` of the *path operation function*. 176 177 **FastAPI** will know that it can use this dependency to define a "security scheme" in the OpenAPI schema (and the automatic API docs). 178 179 /// note | Technical Details 180 181 **FastAPI** will know that it can use the class `OAuth2PasswordBearer` (declared in a dependency) to define the security scheme in OpenAPI because it inherits from `fastapi.security.oauth2.OAuth2`, which in turn inherits from `fastapi.security.base.SecurityBase`. 182 183 All the security utilities that integrate with OpenAPI (and the automatic API docs) inherit from `SecurityBase`, that's how **FastAPI** can know how to integrate them in OpenAPI. 184 185 /// 186 187 ## What it does { #what-it-does } 188 189 It will go and look in the request for that `Authorization` header, check if the value is `Bearer ` plus some token, and will return the token as a `str`. 190 191 If it doesn't see an `Authorization` header, or the value doesn't have a `Bearer ` token, it will respond with a 401 status code error (`UNAUTHORIZED`) directly. 192 193 You don't even have to check if the token exists to return an error. You can be sure that if your function is executed, it will have a `str` in that token. 194 195 You can try it already in the interactive docs: 196 197 198 199 We are not verifying the validity of the token yet, but that's a start already. 200 201 ## Recap { #recap } 202 203 So, in just 3 or 4 extra lines, you already have some primitive form of security. 204

2	
3	In the previous chapter the security system (which is based on the dependency injection system) was giving the *path operation function* a `token` as a `str`:
4	
5	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[12] *}
6	
7	But that is still not that useful.
8	
9	Let's make it give us the current user.
10	
11	## Create a user model { #create-a-user-model }
12	
13	First, let's create a Pydantic user model.
14	
15	The same way we use Pydantic to declare bodies, we can use it anywhere else:
16	
17	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[5,12:16] *}
18	
19	## Create a `get_current_user` dependency { #create-a-get-current-user-dependency }
20	
21	Let's create a dependency `get_current_user`.
22	
23	Remember that dependencies can have sub-dependencies?
24	
25	`get_current_user` will have a dependency with the same `oauth2_scheme` we created before.
26	
27	The same as we were doing before in the *path operation* directly, our new dependency `get_current_user` will receive a `token` as a `str` from the sub-dependency `oauth2_scheme`:
28	
29	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[25] *}
30	
31	## Get the user { #get-the-user }
32	
33	`get_current_user` will use a (fake) utility function we created, that takes a token as a `str` and returns our Pydantic `User` model:
34	
35	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[19:22,26:27] *}
36	
37	## Inject the current user { #inject-the-current-user }
38	
39	So now we can use the same `Depends` with our `get_current_user` in the *path operation*:
40	
41	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[31] *}
42	
43	Notice that we declare the type of `current_user` as the Pydantic model `User`.
44	
45	This will help us inside of the function with all the completion and type checks.
46	
47	/// tip
48	
49	You might remember that request bodies are also declared with Pydantic models.
50	
51	Here **FastAPI** won't get confused because you are using `Depends`.
52	
53	///
54	
55	/// tip
56	
57	The way this dependency system is designed allows us to have different dependencies (different "dependables") that all return a `User` model.
58	
59	We are not restricted to having only one dependency that can return that type of data.
60	
61	///
62	
63	## Other models { #other-models }
64	
65	You can now get the current user directly in the *path operation functions* and deal with the security mechanisms at the **Dependency Injection** level, using `Depends`.
66	
67	And you can use any model or data for the security requirements (in this case, a Pydantic model `User`).
68	
69	But you are not restricted to using some specific data model, class or type.
70	
71	Do you want to have an `id` and `email` and not have any `username` in your model? Sure. You can use these same tools.
72	
73	Do you want to just have a `str`? Or just a `dict`? Or a database class model instance directly? It all works the same way.
74	
75	You actually don't have users that log in to your application but robots, bots, or other systems, that have just an access token? Again, it all works the same.
76	
77	Just use any kind of model, any kind of class, any kind of database that you need for your application. **FastAPI** has you covered with the dependency injection system.
78	
79	## Code size { #code-size }
80	
81	This example might seem verbose. Keep in mind that we are mixing security, data models, utility functions and *path operations* in the same file.
82	
83	But here's the key point.
84	
85	The security and dependency injection stuff is written once.
86	
87	And you can make it as complex as you want. And still, have it written only once, in a single place. With all the flexibility.
88	
89	But you can have thousands of endpoints (*path operations*) using the same security system.
90	
91	And all of them (or any portion of them that you want) can take advantage of re-using these dependencies or any other dependencies you create.
92	
93	And all these thousands of *path operations* can be as small as 3 lines:
94	
95	{* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[30:32] *}
96

100	
101	We are already halfway there.
102	
103	We just need to add a *path operation* for the user/client to actually send the `username` and `password`.
104

toolCalls.result: 1 # Simple OAuth2 with Password and Bearer { #simple-oauth2-with-password-and-bearer } 2 3 Now let's build from the previous chapter and add the missing parts to have a complete security flow. 4 5 ## Get the `username` and `password` { #get-the-username-and-password } 6 7 We are going to use **FastAPI** security utilities to get the `username` and `password`. 8 9 OAuth2 specifies that when using the "password flow" (that we are using) the client/user must send `username` and `password` fields as form data. 10 11 And the spec says that the fields have to be named like that. So `user-name` or `email` wouldn't work. 12 13 But don't worry, you can show it as you wish to your final users in the frontend. 14 15 And your database models can use any other names you want. 16 17 But for the login *path operation*, we need to use these names to be compatible with the spec (and be able to, for example, use the integrated API documentation system). 18 19 The spec also states that the `username` and `password` must be sent as form data (so, no JSON here). 20 21 ### `scope` { #scope } 22 23 The spec also says that the client can send another form field "`scope`". 24 25 The form field name is `scope` (in singular), but it is actually a long string with "scopes" separated by spaces. 26 27 Each "scope" is just a string (without spaces). 28 29 They are normally used to declare specific security permissions, for example: 30 31 * `users:read` or `users:write` are common examples. 32 * `instagram_basic` is used by Facebook / Instagram. 33 * `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive` is used by Google. 34 35 /// note 36 37 In OAuth2 a "scope" is just a string that declares a specific permission required. 38 39 It doesn't matter if it has other characters like `:` or if it is a URL. 40 41 Those details are implementation specific. 42 43 For OAuth2 they are just strings. 44 45 /// 46 47 ## Code to get the `username` and `password` { #code-to-get-the-username-and-password } 48 49 Now let's use the utilities provided by **FastAPI** to handle this. 50 51 ### `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` { #oauth2passwordrequestform } 52 53 First, import `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`, and use it as a dependency with `Depends` in the *path operation* for `/token`: 54 55 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[4,78] *} 56 57 `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` is a class dependency that declares a form body with: 58 59 * The `username`. 60 * The `password`. 61 * An optional `scope` field as a big string, composed of strings separated by spaces. 62 * An optional `grant_type`. 63 64 /// tip 65 66 The OAuth2 spec actually *requires* a field `grant_type` with a fixed value of `password`, but `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` doesn't enforce it. 67 68 If you need to enforce it, use `OAuth2PasswordRequestFormStrict` instead of `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`. 69 70 /// 71 72 * An optional `client_id` (we don't need it for our example). 73 * An optional `client_secret` (we don't need it for our example). 74 75 /// note 76 77 The `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` is not a special class for **FastAPI** as is `OAuth2PasswordBearer`. 78 79 `OAuth2PasswordBearer` makes **FastAPI** know that it is a security scheme. So it is added that way to OpenAPI. 80 81 But `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` is just a class dependency that you could have written yourself, or you could have declared `Form` parameters directly. 82 83 But as it's a common use case, it is provided by **FastAPI** directly, just to make it easier. 84 85 /// 86 87 ### Use the form data { #use-the-form-data } 88 89 /// tip 90 91 The instance of the dependency class `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` won't have an attribute `scope` with the long string separated by spaces, instead, it will have a `scopes` attribute with the actual list of strings for each scope sent. 92 93 We are not using `scopes` in this example, but the functionality is there if you need it. 94 95 /// 96 97 Now, get the user data from the (fake) database, using the `username` from the form field. 98 99 If there is no such user, we return an error saying "Incorrect username or password". 100 101 For the error, we use the exception `HTTPException`: 102 103 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[3,79:81] *} 104 105 ### Check the password { #check-the-password } 106 107 At this point we have the user data from our database, but we haven't checked the password. 108 109 Let's put that data in the Pydantic `UserInDB` model first. 110 111 You should never save plaintext passwords, so, we'll use the (fake) password hashing system. 112 113 If the passwords don't match, we return the same error. 114 115 #### Password hashing { #password-hashing } 116 117 "Hashing" means: converting some content (a password in this case) into a sequence of bytes (just a string) that looks like gibberish. 118 119 Whenever you pass exactly the same content (exactly the same password) you get exactly the same gibberish. 120 121 But you cannot convert from the gibberish back to the password. 122 123 ##### Why use password hashing { #why-use-password-hashing } 124 125 If your database is stolen, the thief won't have your users' plaintext passwords, only the hashes. 126 127 So, the thief won't be able to try to use those same passwords in another system (as many users use the same password everywhere, this would be dangerous). 128 129 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[82:85] *} 130 131 #### About `**user_dict` { #about-user-dict } 132 133 `UserInDB(**user_dict)` means: 134 135 *Pass the keys and values of the `user_dict` directly as key-value arguments, equivalent to:* 136 137 ```Python 138 UserInDB( 139 username = user_dict["username"], 140 email = user_dict["email"], 141 full_name = user_dict["full_name"], 142 disabled = user_dict["disabled"], 143 hashed_password = user_dict["hashed_password"], 144 ) 145 ``` 146 147 /// note 148 149 For a more complete explanation of `**user_dict` check back in [the documentation for **Extra Models**](../extra-models.md#about-user-in-model-dump). 150 151 /// 152 153 ## Return the token { #return-the-token } 154 155 The response of the `token` endpoint must be a JSON object. 156 157 It should have a `token_type`. In our case, as we are using "Bearer" tokens, the token type should be "`bearer`". 158 159 And it should have an `access_token`, with a string containing our access token. 160 161 For this simple example, we are going to just be completely insecure and return the same `username` as the token. 162 163 /// tip 164 165 In the next chapter, you will see a real secure implementation, with password hashing and JWT tokens. 166 167 But for now, let's focus on the specific details we need. 168 169 /// 170 171 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[87] *} 172 173 /// tip 174 175 By the spec, you should return a JSON with an `access_token` and a `token_type`, the same as in this example. 176 177 This is something that you have to do yourself in your code, and make sure you use those JSON keys. 178 179 It's almost the only thing that you have to remember to do correctly yourself, to be compliant with the specifications. 180 181 For the rest, **FastAPI** handles it for you. 182 183 /// 184 185 ## Update the dependencies { #update-the-dependencies } 186 187 Now we are going to update our dependencies. 188 189 We want to get the `current_user` *only* if this user is active. 190 191 So, we create an additional dependency `get_current_active_user` that in turn uses `get_current_user` as a dependency. 192 193 Both of these dependencies will just return an HTTP error if the user doesn't exist, or is inactive. 194 195 So, in our endpoint, we will only get a user if the user exists, was correctly authenticated, and is active: 196 197 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[58:66,69:74,94] *} 198 199 /// note 200 201 The additional header `WWW-Authenticate` with value `Bearer` we are returning here is also part of the spec. 202 203 Any HTTP (error) status code 401 "UNAUTHORIZED" is supposed to also return a `WWW-Authenticate` header. 204 205 In the case of bearer tokens (our case), the value of that header should be `Bearer`. 206 207 You can actually skip that extra header and it would still work. 208 209 But it's provided here to be compliant with the specifications. 210 211 Also, there might be tools that expect and use it (now or in the future) and that might be useful for you or your users, now or in the future. 212 213 That's the benefit of standards... 214 215 /// 216 217 ## See it in action { #see-it-in-action } 218 219 Open the interactive docs: [http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs](http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs). 220 221 ### Authenticate { #authenticate } 222 223 Click the "Authorize" button. 224 225 Use the credentials: 226 227 User: `johndoe` 228 229 Password: `secret` 230 231 232 233 After authenticating in the system, you will see it like: 234 235 236 237 ### Get your own user data { #get-your-own-user-data } 238 239 Now use the operation `GET` with the path `/users/me`. 240 241 You will get your user's data, like: 242 243 ```JSON 244 { 245 "username": "johndoe", 246 "email": "johndoe@example.com", 247 "full_name": "John Doe", 248 "disabled": false, 249 "hashed_password": "fakehashedsecret" 250 } 251 ``` 252 253 254 255 If you click the lock icon and logout, and then try the same operation again, you will get an HTTP 401 error of: 256 257 ```JSON 258 { 259 "detail": "Not authenticated" 260 } 261 ``` 262 263 ### Inactive user { #inactive-user } 264 265 Now try with an inactive user, authenticate with: 266 267 User: `alice` 268 269 Password: `secret2` 270 271 And try to use the operation `GET` with the path `/users/me`. 272 273 You will get an "Inactive user" error, like: 274 275 ```JSON 276 { 277 "detail": "Inactive user" 278 } 279 ``` 280 281 ## Recap { #recap } 282 283 You now have the tools to implement a complete security system based on `username` and `password` for your API. 284 285 Using these tools, you can make the security system compatible with any database and with any user or data model. 286 287 The only detail missing is that it is not actually "secure" yet. 288 289 In the next chapter you'll see how to use a secure password hashing library and JWT tokens. 290
