1 # OAuth2 with Password (and hashing), Bearer with JWT tokens { #oauth2-with-password-and-hashing-bearer-with-jwt-tokens } 2 3 Now that we have all the security flow, let's make the application actually secure, using JWT tokens and secure password hashing. 4 5 This code is something you can actually use in your application, save the password hashes in your database, etc. 6 7 We are going to start from where we left in the previous chapter and increment it. 8 9 ## About JWT { #about-jwt } 10 11 JWT means "JSON Web Tokens". 12 13 It's a standard to codify a JSON object in a long dense string without spaces. It looks like this: 14 15 ``` 16 eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c 17 ``` 18 19 It is not encrypted, so, anyone could recover the information from the contents. 20 21 But it's signed. So, when you receive a token that you issued, you can verify that it was you who issued it. 22 23 That way, you can create a token with an expiration of, let's say, 1 week. And then when the user comes back the next day with the token, you know that user is still logged in to your system. 24 25 After a week, the token will be expired and the user will not be authorized and will have to sign in again to get a new token. And if the user (or a third party) tried to modify the token to change the expiration, you would be able to discover it, because the signatures would not match. 26 27 If you want to play with JWT tokens and see how they work, check [https://jwt.io](https://jwt.io/). 28 29 ## Install `PyJWT` { #install-pyjwt } 30 31 We need to install `PyJWT` to generate and verify the JWT tokens in Python. 32 33 Add `pyjwt` to your project: 34 35
36 37 ```console 38 $ uv add pyjwt 39 40 ---> 100% 41 ``` 42 43
44 45 /// note 46 47 If you are planning to use digital signature algorithms like RSA or ECDSA, you should install the cryptography library dependency `pyjwt[crypto]`. 48 49 You can read more about it in the [PyJWT Installation docs](https://pyjwt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/installation.html). 50 51 /// 52 53 ## Password hashing { #password-hashing } 54 55 "Hashing" means converting some content (a password in this case) into a sequence of bytes (just a string) that looks like gibberish. 56 57 Whenever you pass exactly the same content (exactly the same password) you get exactly the same gibberish. 58 59 But you cannot convert from the gibberish back to the password. 60 61 ### Why use password hashing { #why-use-password-hashing } 62 63 If your database is stolen, the thief won't have your users' plaintext passwords, only the hashes. 64 65 So, the thief won't be able to try to use that password in another system (as many users use the same password everywhere, this would be dangerous). 66 67 ## Install `pwdlib` { #install-pwdlib } 68 69 pwdlib is a great Python package to handle password hashes. 70 71 It supports many secure hashing algorithms and utilities to work with them. 72 73 The recommended algorithm is "Argon2". 74 75 Add `pwdlib` with Argon2 to your project: 76 77
78 79 ```console 80 $ uv add "pwdlib[argon2]" 81 82 ---> 100% 83 ``` 84 85
86 87 /// tip 88 89 With `pwdlib`, you could even configure it to be able to read passwords created by **Django**, a **Flask** security plug-in or many others. 90 91 So, you would be able to, for example, share the same data from a Django application in a database with a FastAPI application. Or gradually migrate a Django application using the same database. 92 93 And your users would be able to login from your Django app or from your **FastAPI** app, at the same time. 94 95 /// 96 97 ## Hash and verify the passwords { #hash-and-verify-the-passwords } 98 99 Import the tools we need from `pwdlib`. 100 101 Create a PasswordHash instance with recommended settings - it will be used for hashing and verifying passwords. 102 103 /// tip 104 105 pwdlib also supports the bcrypt hashing algorithm but does not include legacy algorithms - for working with outdated hashes, it is recommended to use the passlib library. 106 107 For example, you could use it to read and verify passwords generated by another system (like Django) but hash any new passwords with a different algorithm like Argon2 or Bcrypt. 108 109 And be compatible with all of them at the same time. 110 111 /// 112 113 Create a utility function to hash a password coming from the user. 114 115 And another utility to verify if a received password matches the hash stored. 116 117 And another one to authenticate and return a user. 118 119 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[8,49,51,58:59,62:63,72:79] *} 120 121 When `authenticate_user` is called with a username that doesn't exist in the database, we still run `verify_password` against a dummy hash. 122 123 This ensures the endpoint takes roughly the same amount of time to respond whether the username is valid or not, preventing **timing attacks** that could be used to enumerate existing usernames. 124 125 /// note 126 127 If you check the new (fake) database `fake_users_db`, you will see what the hashed password looks like now: `"$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$wagCPXjifgvUFBzq4hqe3w$CYaIb8sB+wtD+Vu/P4uod1+Qof8h+1g7bbDlBID48Rc"`. 128 129 /// 130 131 ## Handle JWT tokens { #handle-jwt-tokens } 132 133 Import the modules installed. 134 135 Create a random secret key that will be used to sign the JWT tokens. 136 137 To generate a secure random secret key use the command: 138 139
140 141 ```console 142 $ openssl rand -hex 32 143 144 09d25e094faa6ca2556c818166b7a9563b93f7099f6f0f4caa6cf63b88e8d3e7 145 ``` 146 147
148 149 And copy the output to the variable `SECRET_KEY` (don't use the one in the example). 150 151 Create a variable `ALGORITHM` with the algorithm used to sign the JWT token and set it to `"HS256"`. 152 153 Create a variable for the expiration of the token. 154 155 Define a Pydantic Model that will be used in the token endpoint for the response. 156 157 Create a utility function to generate a new access token. 158 159 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[4,7,13:15,29:31,82:90] *} 160 161 ## Update the dependencies { #update-the-dependencies } 162 163 Update `get_current_user` to receive the same token as before, but this time, using JWT tokens. 164 165 Decode the received token, verify it, and return the current user. 166 167 If the token is invalid, return an HTTP error right away. 168 169 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[93:110] *} 170 171 ## Update the `/token` *path operation* { #update-the-token-path-operation } 172 173 Create a `timedelta` with the expiration time of the token. 174 175 Create a real JWT access token and return it. 176 177 {* ../../docs_src/security/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[121:136] *} 178 179 ### Technical details about the JWT "subject" `sub` { #technical-details-about-the-jwt-subject-sub } 180 181 The JWT specification says that there's a key `sub`, with the subject of the token. 182 183 It's optional to use it, but that's where you would put the user's identification, so we are using it here. 184 185 JWT might be used for other things apart from identifying a user and allowing them to perform operations directly on your API. 186 187 For example, you could identify a "car" or a "blog post". 188 189 Then you could add permissions about that entity, like "drive" (for the car) or "edit" (for the blog). 190 191 And then, you could give that JWT token to a user (or bot), and they could use it to perform those actions (drive the car, or edit the blog post) without even needing to have an account, just with the JWT token your API generated for that. 192 193 Using these ideas, JWT can be used for way more sophisticated scenarios. 194 195 In those cases, several of those entities could have the same ID, let's say `foo` (a user `foo`, a car `foo`, and a blog post `foo`). 196 197 So, to avoid ID collisions, when creating the JWT token for the user, you could prefix the value of the `sub` key, e.g. with `username:`. So, in this example, the value of `sub` could have been: `username:johndoe`. 198 199 The important thing to keep in mind is that the `sub` key should have a unique identifier across the entire application, and it should be a string. 200 201 ## Check it { #check-it } 202 203 Run the server and go to the docs: [http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs](http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs). 204 205 You'll see the user interface like: 206 207 208 209 Authorize the application the same way as before. 210 211 Using the credentials: 212 213 Username: `johndoe` 214 Password: `secret` 215 216 /// tip 217 218 Notice that nowhere in the code is the plaintext password "`secret`", we only have the hashed version. 219 220 /// 221 222 223 224 Call the endpoint `/users/me/`, you will get the response as: 225 226 ```JSON 227 { 228 "username": "johndoe", 229 "email": "johndoe@example.com", 230 "full_name": "John Doe", 231 "disabled": false 232 } 233 ``` 234 235 236 237 If you open the developer tools, you could see how the data sent only includes the token, the password is only sent in the first request to authenticate the user and get that access token, but not afterwards: 238 239 240 241 /// note 242 243 Notice the header `Authorization`, with a value that starts with `Bearer `. 244 245 /// 246 247 ## Advanced usage with `scopes` { #advanced-usage-with-scopes } 248 249 OAuth2 has the notion of "scopes". 250 251 You can use them to add a specific set of permissions to a JWT token. 252 253 Then you can give this token to a user directly or a third party, to interact with your API with a set of restrictions. 254 255 You can learn how to use them and how they are integrated into **FastAPI** later in the **Advanced User Guide**. 256 257 ## Recap { #recap } 258 259 With what you have seen up to now, you can set up a secure **FastAPI** application using standards like OAuth2 and JWT. 260 261 In almost any framework handling the security becomes a rather complex subject quite quickly. 262 263 Many packages that simplify it a lot have to make many compromises with the data model, database, and available features. And some of these packages that simplify things too much actually have security flaws underneath. 264 265 --- 266 267 **FastAPI** doesn't make any compromise with any database, data model or tool. 268 269 It gives you all the flexibility to choose the ones that fit your project the best. 270 271 And you can use directly many well maintained and widely used packages like `pwdlib` and `PyJWT`, because **FastAPI** doesn't require any complex mechanisms to integrate external packages. 272 273 But it provides you the tools to simplify the process as much as possible without compromising flexibility, robustness, or security. 274 275 And you can use and implement secure, standard protocols, like OAuth2 in a relatively simple way. 276 277 You can learn more in the **Advanced User Guide** about how to use OAuth2 "scopes", for a more fine-grained permission system, following these same standards. OAuth2 with scopes is the mechanism used by many big authentication providers, like Facebook, Google, GitHub, Microsoft, X (Twitter), etc. to authorize third party applications to interact with their APIs on behalf of their users. 278

79-### Dependencies with `yield` and `scope` { #dependencies-with-yield-and-scope }

81-In version 0.121.0, FastAPI added support for `Depends(scope="function")` for dependencies with `yield`.
82-
83-Using `Depends(scope="function")`, the exit code after `yield` is executed right after the *path operation function* is finished, before the response is sent back to the client.

85-And when using `Depends(scope="request")` (the default), the exit code after `yield` is executed after the response is sent.

1	# Security { #security }
2	
3	There are many ways to handle security, authentication and authorization.
4	
5	And it normally is a complex and "difficult" topic.
6	
7	In many frameworks and systems just handling security and authentication takes a big amount of effort and code (in many cases it can be 50% or more of all the code written).
8	
9	**FastAPI** provides several tools to help you deal with **Security** easily, rapidly, in a standard way, without having to study and learn all the security specifications.
10	
11	But first, let's check some small concepts.
12	
13	## In a hurry? { #in-a-hurry }
14	
15	If you don't care about any of these terms and you just need to add security with authentication based on username and password *right now*, skip to the next chapters.
16	
17	## OAuth2 { #oauth2 }
18	
19	OAuth2 is a specification that defines several ways to handle authentication and authorization.
20	
21	It is quite an extensive specification and covers several complex use cases.
22	
23	It includes ways to authenticate using a "third party".
24	
25	That's what all the systems with "login with Facebook, Google, X (Twitter), GitHub" use underneath.
26	
27	### OAuth 1 { #oauth-1 }
28	
29	There was an OAuth 1, which is very different from OAuth2, and more complex, as it included direct specifications on how to encrypt the communication.
30	
31	It is not very popular or used nowadays.
32	
33	OAuth2 doesn't specify how to encrypt the communication, it expects you to have your application served with HTTPS.
34	
35	/// tip
36	
37	In the section about **deployment** you will see how to set up HTTPS for free, using Traefik and Let's Encrypt.
38	
39	///
40	
41	## OpenID Connect { #openid-connect }
42	
43	OpenID Connect is another specification, based on **OAuth2**.
44	
45	It just extends OAuth2 specifying some things that are relatively ambiguous in OAuth2, to try to make it more interoperable.
46	
47	For example, Google login uses OpenID Connect (which underneath uses OAuth2).
48	
49	But Facebook login doesn't support OpenID Connect. It has its own flavor of OAuth2.
50	
51	### OpenID (not "OpenID Connect") { #openid-not-openid-connect }
52	
53	There was also an "OpenID" specification. That tried to solve the same thing as **OpenID Connect**, but was not based on OAuth2.
54	
55	So, it was a complete additional system.
56	
57	It is not very popular or used nowadays.
58	
59	## OpenAPI { #openapi }
60	
61	OpenAPI (previously known as Swagger) is the open specification for building APIs (now part of the Linux Foundation).
62	
63	**FastAPI** is based on **OpenAPI**.
64	
65	That's what makes it possible to have multiple automatic interactive documentation interfaces, code generation, etc.
66	
67	OpenAPI has a way to define multiple security "schemes".
68	
69	By using them, you can take advantage of all these standard-based tools, including these interactive documentation systems.
70	
71	OpenAPI defines the following security schemes:
72	
73	* `apiKey`: an application specific key that can come from:
74	    * A query parameter.
75	    * A header.
76	    * A cookie.
77	* `http`: standard HTTP authentication systems, including:
78	    * `bearer`: a header `Authorization` with a value of `Bearer ` plus a token. This is inherited from OAuth2.
79	    * HTTP Basic authentication.
80	    * HTTP Digest, etc.
81	* `oauth2`: all the OAuth2 ways to handle security (called "flows").
82	    * Several of these flows are appropriate for building an OAuth 2.0 authentication provider (like Google, Facebook, X (Twitter), GitHub, etc):
83	        * `implicit`
84	        * `clientCredentials`
85	        * `authorizationCode`
86	    * But there is one specific "flow" that can be perfectly used for handling authentication in the same application directly:
87	        * `password`: some next chapters will cover examples of this.
88	* `openIdConnect`: has a way to define how to discover OAuth2 authentication data automatically.
89	    * This automatic discovery is what is defined in the OpenID Connect specification.
90	
91	
92	/// tip
93	
94	Integrating other authentication/authorization providers like Google, Facebook, X (Twitter), GitHub, etc. is also possible and relatively easy.
95	
96	The most complex problem is building an authentication/authorization provider like those, but **FastAPI** gives you the tools to do it easily, while doing the heavy lifting for you.
97	
98	///
99	
100	## **FastAPI** utilities { #fastapi-utilities }
101	
102	FastAPI provides several tools for each of these security schemes in the `fastapi.security` module that simplify using these security mechanisms.
103	
104	In the next chapters you will see how to add security to your API using those tools provided by **FastAPI**.
105	
106	And you will also see how it gets automatically integrated into the interactive documentation system.
107

### Dependencies with `yield` and `except`, Technical Details { #dependencies-with-yield-and-except-technical-details }

Before FastAPI 0.110.0, if you used a dependency with `yield`, and then you captured an exception with `except` in that dependency, and you didn't raise the exception again, the exception would be automatically raised/forwarded to any exception handlers or the internal server error handler.

This was changed in version 0.110.0 to fix unhandled memory consumption from forwarded exceptions without a handler (internal server errors), and to make it consistent with the behavior of regular Python code.

### Background Tasks and Dependencies with `yield`, Technical Details { #background-tasks-and-dependencies-with-yield-technical-details }

Before FastAPI 0.106.0, raising exceptions after `yield` was not possible, the exit code in dependencies with `yield` was executed *after* the response was sent, so [Exception Handlers](../tutorial/handling-errors.md#install-custom-exception-handlers) would have already run.

This was designed this way mainly to allow using the same objects "yielded" by dependencies inside of background tasks, because the exit code would be executed after the background tasks were finished.

This was changed in FastAPI 0.106.0 with the intention to not hold resources while waiting for the response to travel through the network.

/// tip

Additionally, a background task is normally an independent set of logic that should be handled separately, with its own resources (e.g. its own database connection).

So, this way you will probably have cleaner code.

///

If you used to rely on this behavior, now you should create the resources for background tasks inside the background task itself, and use internally only data that doesn't depend on the resources of dependencies with `yield`.

For example, instead of using the same database session, you would create a new database session inside of the background task, and you would obtain the objects from the database using this new session. And then instead of passing the object from the database as a parameter to the background task function, you would pass the ID of that object and then obtain the object again inside the background task function.

# FastAPI Tutorial — Dependencies & Security (kondensierte Notizen)

Quelle: `docs/en/docs/tutorial/{dependencies,security}/*.md` + `docs_src/{dependencies,security}/*_an_py310.py` (master, Stand jetzt). Alle Snippets sind wörtlich aus den `docs_src`-Dateien.

---

## 1. `dependencies/index` — Dependency Injection Grundlagen

**Kernidee:** Path-Operation-Funktionen deklarieren, was sie brauchen; FastAPI löst es auf und "injiziert" es. Zweck: geteilte Logik, DB-Connections, Auth/Rollen — ohne Code-Duplikation.

**„Dependable"** = die Dependency selbst: *irgendein Callable*, das Parameter genauso deklariert wie eine Path-Operation-Funktion. Wörtlich: „You can think of it as a *path operation function* without the decorator." FastAPI analysiert die **Signatur** identisch zu einer Path Operation → Query/Path/Header/Cookie/Body/Sub-Dependencies, inkl. Validierung, Konvertierung **und OpenAPI-Schema** (Dependency-Parameter tauchen in `/docs` auf).

`Depends()` bekommt **genau ein** Argument, und man **ruft die Funktion nicht auf** (keine Klammern): `Depends(common_parameters)`, nicht `Depends(common_parameters())`.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
    return commons
```

Pro Request: FastAPI ruft die Dependency mit den korrekten Parametern auf → Rückgabewert wird dem Parameter zugewiesen.

**Wiederverwendbarer Type-Alias** (empfohlen gegen Duplikation; reines Standard-Python, kein FastAPI-Feature — Typinfo bleibt für Editor/mypy erhalten):

```python
CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep): ...

@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep): ...
```

`async def` und `def` sind frei mischbar (async Dependency in def-Path-Op und umgekehrt). `Annotated`-Support ab FastAPI 0.95.0 (min. 0.95.1 empfohlen). Andere Namen für dasselbe Konzept: resources, providers, services, injectables, components.

---

## 2. `dependencies/classes-as-dependencies`

**Kernidee:** Der entscheidende Faktor ist nicht „Funktion", sondern **callable**. Eine Klasse ist callable (`Cat(name="x")`), also kann sie Dependency sein — FastAPI inspiziert dann die Parameter von `__init__`. Vorteil gegenüber `dict`: Editor-Autocompletion/Typprüfung auf dem Ergebnis.

```python
class CommonQueryParams:
    def __init__(self, q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
        self.q = q
        self.skip = skip
        self.limit = limit

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends(CommonQueryParams)]):
    ...
```

Wichtig: **nur das Argument in `Depends(...)` zählt** für FastAPI (daraus werden Parameter extrahiert, das wird aufgerufen). Der erste Typ im `Annotated` ist rein für Editor/Typchecker — `Annotated[Any, Depends(CommonQueryParams)]` funktioniert genauso, ist aber schlechter für Tooling.

**Shortcut** (nur wenn die Dependency *exakt die Klasse selbst* ist, die instanziiert werden soll):

```python
commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends()]
```

`Depends()` ohne Argument → FastAPI nimmt den Typ aus dem `Annotated`. (Non-Annotated-Variante: `commons: CommonQueryParams = Depends()` — Doku empfiehlt durchgehend die `Annotated`-Form.) Auch Callables ohne Parameter sind erlaubt.

---

## 3. `dependencies/sub-dependencies`

Dependencies dürfen selbst Dependencies haben, beliebig tief. Eine Funktion ist dann gleichzeitig „dependable" und „dependant". FastAPI löst den Baum in korrekter Reihenfolge auf.

```python
from fastapi import Cookie, Depends, FastAPI

def query_extractor(q: str | None = None):
    return q

def query_or_cookie_extractor(
    q: Annotated[str, Depends(query_extractor)],
    last_query: Annotated[str | None, Cookie()] = None,
):
    if not q:
        return last_query
    return q

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_query(query_or_default: Annotated[str, Depends(query_or_cookie_extractor)]):
    return {"q_or_cookie": query_or_default}
```

Die Path Operation deklariert nur die äußere Dependency; `query_extractor` wird von FastAPI vorher gelöst und durchgereicht.

**Caching pro Request (wichtig!):** Wird dieselbe Dependency mehrfach für dieselbe Path Operation gebraucht (z. B. gemeinsame Sub-Dependency zweier Dependencies), ruft FastAPI sie **nur einmal pro Request** auf und cached den Rückgabewert für alle Dependants dieses Requests. Zum Abschalten:

```python
async def needy_dependency(fresh_value: Annotated[str, Depends(get_value, use_cache=False)]):
    return {"fresh_value": fresh_value}
```

---

## 4. `dependencies/dependencies-in-path-operation-decorators`

**Wann:** Man braucht den Rückgabewert nicht (oder es gibt keinen), die Dependency soll aber ausgeführt/geprüft werden — typisch Auth-/Header-Checks. Vermeidet außerdem „unused parameter"-Warnungen von Editoren.

```python
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException

async def verify_token(x_token: Annotated[str, Header()]):
    if x_token != "fake-super-secret-token":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="X-Token header invalid")

async def verify_key(x_key: Annotated[str, Header()]):
    if x_key != "fake-super-secret-key":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="X-Key header invalid")
    return x_key

@app.get("/items/", dependencies=[Depends(verify_token), Depends(verify_key)])
async def read_items():
    return [{"item": "Foo"}, {"item": "Bar"}]
```

`dependencies=` ist eine **Liste von `Depends()`**. Diese Dependencies dürfen Request-Anforderungen deklarieren (Header, Sub-Dependencies), Exceptions werfen, und dürfen Werte zurückgeben — die Werte werden schlicht **verworfen** (normale, anderswo genutzte Dependencies sind also wiederverwendbar).

---

## 5. `dependencies/global-dependencies`

Gilt für **alle** Path Operations der App:

```python
app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(verify_token), Depends(verify_key)])
```

Gleiche Semantik wie im Decorator, nur app-weit.

**Auf `APIRouter`-Ebene** (aus `bigger-applications`, gleiches Muster für Gruppen):

```python
router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/items",
    tags=["items"],
    dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)],
    responses={404: {"description": "Not found"}},
)
```

oder erst beim Einbinden (Original-Router bleibt unverändert):

```python
app.include_router(
    admin.router,
    prefix="/admin",
    tags=["admin"],
    dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)],
    responses={418: {"description": "I'm a teapot"}},
)
```

**Ausführungsreihenfolge:** Router-Dependencies → Decorator-`dependencies` → normale Parameter-Dependencies. Globale App-Dependencies werden mit den Router-Dependencies kombiniert (sie ersetzen sie nicht).

---

## 6. `dependencies/dependencies-with-yield`

**Kernidee:** `yield` statt `return` → Code **vor/inkl. `yield`** = Setup (läuft vor der Response), yielded value wird injiziert, Code **nach `yield`** = Teardown/Exit-Code. Genau **ein** `yield` pro Dependency. `async def` und `def` beide erlaubt.

```python
async def get_db():
    db = DBSession()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
```

**Context-Manager-Bezug:** Jede Funktion, die für `@contextlib.contextmanager` / `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` gültig wäre, ist als FastAPI-Dependency gültig — FastAPI benutzt genau diese beiden Dekoratoren intern und baut daraus einen Context Manager. Man soll die Dekoratoren **nicht** selbst setzen. `with`/`async with` *innerhalb* der Dependency ist dagegen erlaubt:

```python
class MySuperContextManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.db = DBSession()
    def __enter__(self):
        return self.db
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        self.db.close()

async def get_db():
    with MySuperContextManager() as db:
        yield db
```

**Exception-Verhalten:** Eine Exception, die irgendwo danach geworfen wird (in einer weiteren Dependency oder in der Path-Operation-Funktion, **inklusive `HTTPException`**), kommt an der `yield`-Stelle wieder heraus → mit `except SomeException` abfangbar, `finally` garantiert Teardown.

```python
def get_username():
    try:
        yield "Rick"
    except OwnerError as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=f"Owner error: {e}")
```

**Aktuelle Regel „immer re-raisen":** Fängt man eine Exception mit `except` ab und wirft **nicht** neu (weder dieselbe noch z. B. eine `HTTPException`), merkt FastAPI nichts davon — genau wie normales Python. Der Client bekommt zwar 500, aber der **Server hat keinerlei Log**. Deshalb: entweder eine `HTTPException`/ähnliches werfen oder die Originalexception mit nacktem `raise` erneut werfen.

```python
def get_username():
    try:
        yield "Rick"
    except InternalError:
        print("We don't swallow the internal error here, we raise again 😎")
        raise
```

(Historie: Vor 0.110.0 wurde eine geschluckte Exception automatisch weitergereicht; seit 0.110.0 nicht mehr — konsistent mit normalem Python. Für custom Responses auf Exceptions → Custom Exception Handler statt dieser Technik.)

**Reihenfolge des Exit-Codes bei Sub-Dependencies:** `dependency_c` → `dependency_b` → `dependency_a`; FastAPI garantiert, dass beim Exit von `c` der Wert von `b` (und beim Exit von `b` der von `a`) noch verfügbar ist, d. h. Teardown läuft in **umgekehrter Reihenfolge** zum Setup (LIFO, Context-Manager-Stack).

```python
async def dependency_a():
    dep_a = generate_dep_a()
    try:
        yield dep_a
    finally:
        dep_a.close()

async def dependency_b(dep_a: Annotated[DepA, Depends(dependency_a)]):
    dep_b = generate_dep_b()
    try:
        yield dep_b
    finally:
        dep_b.close(dep_a)

async def dependency_c(dep_b: Annotated[DepB, Depends(dependency_b)]):
    dep_c = generate_dep_c()
    try:
        yield dep_c
    finally:
        dep_c.close(dep_b)
```

**Wann läuft der Exit-Code — `scope` (neu, FastAPI ≥ 0.121.0):** Default ist **nach dem Senden der Response**.

```python
def get_username():
    try:
        yield "Rick"
    finally:
        print("Cleanup up before response is sent")

@app.get("/users/me")
def get_user_me(username: Annotated[str, Depends(get_username, scope="function")]):
    return username
```

- `scope="request"` (Default bei `yield`): Dependency umschließt den **kompletten Request/Response-Zyklus**, Exit **nach** dem Senden der Response (nötig z. B. für DB-Session in `StreamingResponse`).
- `scope="function"`: Exit direkt nach Ende der Path-Operation-Funktion, **vor** dem Senden der Response (frühes Freigeben von Ressourcen).
- Regel für Sub-Dependencies: `scope="request"` darf **nur** `request`-Sub-Dependencies haben; `scope="function"` darf beides haben (eine Dependency muss ihren Exit-Code vor dem ihrer Sub-Dependencies ausführen können).

Nur **eine** Response wird gesendet; ist sie raus, ist sie nicht mehr änderbar. Versionsgeschichte: <0.106 Exit nach Response (raise nach `yield` unmöglich); 0.106–0.117 Exit vor Response; ab 0.118.0 wieder nach der Response; 0.121.0 bringt `scope`. Für Background Tasks: eigene Ressourcen im Task erzeugen, nicht die geyieldeten mitbenutzen (z. B. Objekt-ID statt Objekt übergeben).

---

## 7. `security/index` — Begriffe

OAuth2 = Spezifikation für Authentifizierung/Autorisierung mit mehreren „Flows"; verschlüsselt selbst nichts → HTTPS vorausgesetzt. OpenID Connect = Erweiterung auf OAuth2-Basis (Google-Login; Facebook nutzt eigenen OAuth2-Dialekt). OpenAPI (ex-Swagger) definiert Security Schemes: `apiKey` (Query/Header/Cookie), `http` (u. a. `bearer`, Basic, Digest), `oauth2` (Flows `implicit`, `clientCredentials`, `authorizationCode`, **`password`** ← der für eigene Apps passende), `openIdConnect`. FastAPI-Werkzeuge liegen in `fastapi.security`.

---

## 8. `security/first-steps` — `OAuth2PasswordBearer`

**Password-Flow (vereinfacht):** Frontend schickt `username`+`password` als Form-Data an `tokenUrl` → API antwortet mit Token → Frontend speichert Token → schickt bei Folge-Requests Header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

app = FastAPI()

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    return {"token": token}
```

**Was `OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")` tatsächlich tut:**
1. Erzeugt eine **callable Instanz** → direkt in `Depends()` verwendbar.
2. Zur Request-Zeit: liest den `Authorization`-Header, prüft auf `Bearer <token>` und **gibt den Token als `str` zurück**. Fehlt der Header oder ist er kein Bearer → sofort **401 UNAUTHORIZED**, die eigene Funktion läuft gar nicht erst (im Funktionskörper ist `token` garantiert ein `str`). Der Token wird hier **noch nicht validiert**.
3. Deklariert das **OpenAPI Security Scheme** — weil `OAuth2PasswordBearer` von `fastapi.security.oauth2.OAuth2` und damit von `fastapi.security.base.SecurityBase` erbt. Das erzeugt in Swagger den **„Authorize"-Button** + Schloss-Symbol an der Operation.
4. `tokenUrl` **erzeugt kein Endpoint**, es dokumentiert nur, wohin der Client Credentials schicken soll. Relative URL (`"token"` ≙ `./token`) ist wichtig für Betrieb hinter einem Proxy. camelCase, weil OpenAPI-Spec-Name.

Form-Data → `python-multipart` nötig (in `fastapi[standard]` enthalten, sonst `uv add python-multipart`).

---

## 9. `security/get-current-user` — Depends-Kette

```python
class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str | None = None
    full_name: str | None = None
    disabled: bool | None = None

def fake_decode_token(token):
    return User(username=token + "fakedecoded", email="john@example.com", full_name="John Doe")

async def get_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    user = fake_decode_token(token)
    return user

@app.get("/users/me")
async def read_users_me(current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)]):
    return current_user
```

`get_current_user` ist eine ganz normale Dependency mit `oauth2_scheme` als Sub-Dependency. FastAPI verwechselt das Pydantic-Modell **nicht** mit einem Request-Body, weil `Depends` benutzt wird. Rückgabetyp ist frei (Pydantic-Modell, `dict`, `str`, DB-Objekt …); Sicherheitslogik wird einmal geschrieben, tausende Endpoints bleiben 3-Zeiler.

---

## 10. `security/simple-oauth2` — `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`, Token-Response, 401-Header

**`OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`** (aus `fastapi.security`) ist eine **Klassen-Dependency**, die einen Form-Body deklariert mit:
- `username` (Pflicht), `password` (Pflicht) — Namen sind von der Spec vorgeschrieben (`email`/`user-name` wären nicht konform), Übertragung als **Form-Data, nicht JSON**
- `scope` — optional, **ein einziger String** mit leerzeichengetrennten Scopes; die Instanz hat aber das Attribut **`scopes`** (Liste von Strings). Scopes sind beliebige Strings, z. B. `users:read`, `instagram_basic`, `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive`
- `grant_type` — optional; Spec verlangt fix `password`, wird hier **nicht** erzwungen → `OAuth2PasswordRequestFormStrict` erzwingt es
- `client_id`, `client_secret` — optional

Kein FastAPI-Sonderfall (anders als `OAuth2PasswordBearer`): es landet **nicht** als Security Scheme in OpenAPI, man hätte es mit `Form`-Parametern selbst schreiben können.

```python
@app.post("/token")
async def login(form_data: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()]):
    user_dict = fake_users_db.get(form_data.username)
    if not user_dict:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Incorrect username or password")
    user = UserInDB(**user_dict)
    hashed_password = fake_hash_password(form_data.password)
    if not hashed_password == user.hashed_password:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Incorrect username or password")

    return {"access_token": user.username, "token_type": "bearer"}
```

**Pflicht-Response-Shape** des Token-Endpoints (JSON): `{"access_token": "<str>", "token_type": "bearer"}` — „almost the only thing that you have to remember to do correctly yourself" (die Keys müssen exakt so heißen).

**Kette `get_current_user` → `get_current_active_user`** + `WWW-Authenticate`:

```python
async def get_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    user = fake_decode_token(token)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Not authenticated",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    return user

async def get_current_active_user(
    current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)],
):
    if current_user.disabled:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Inactive user")
    return current_user

@app.get("/users/me")
async def read_users_me(current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_active_user)]):
    return current_user
```

**`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`**: Teil der Spec — jede 401 soll diesen Header mitliefern; bei Bearer-Tokens ist der Wert `Bearer`. Technisch optional („you can actually skip that extra header and it would still work"), aber standardkonform. „Inactive user" ist bewusst **400**, nicht 401.

---

## 11. `security/oauth2-jwt` — JWT + echtes Password-Hashing

**JWT:** JSON in einem langen, dichten String, **nicht verschlüsselt** (Inhalt für jeden lesbar), aber **signiert** → Manipulation (z. B. an `exp`) wird erkannt.

**Bibliotheken (aktueller Stand der Doku):**
- **PyJWT** (`uv add pyjwt`; `import jwt`) — für RSA/ECDSA zusätzlich `pyjwt[crypto]`.
- **pwdlib** (`uv add "pwdlib[argon2]"`) — **das ist, was die aktuelle Doku verwendet**; empfohlener Algorithmus **Argon2**. `passlib` wird nur noch als Empfehlung für **Legacy-Hashes** erwähnt (pwdlib unterstützt auch bcrypt, aber keine Alt-Algorithmen).

Setup & Konstanten:

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import jwt
from jwt.exceptions import InvalidTokenError
from pwdlib import PasswordHash

# to get a string like this run:
# openssl rand -hex 32
SECRET_KEY = "09d25e094faa6ca2556c818166b7a9563b93f7099f6f0f4caa6cf63b88e8d3e7"
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 30

password_hash = PasswordHash.recommended()
DUMMY_HASH = password_hash.hash("dummypassword")
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

class Token(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    token_type: str

class TokenData(BaseModel):
    username: str | None = None
```

Hash-/Verify-Utilities + `authenticate_user` (mit Timing-Attack-Schutz):

```python
def verify_password(plain_password, hashed_password):
    return password_hash.verify(plain_password, hashed_password)

def get_password_hash(password):
    return password_hash.hash(password)

def authenticate_user(fake_db, username: str, password: str):
    user = get_user(fake_db, username)
    if not user:
        verify_password(password, DUMMY_HASH)   # gleiche Laufzeit → keine User-Enumeration
        return False
    if not verify_password(password, user.hashed_password):
        return False
    return user
```

Gespeicherter Hash sieht so aus: `"$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$wagCPXjifgvUFBzq4hqe3w$CYaIb8sB+wtD+Vu/P4uod1+Qof8h+1g7bbDlBID48Rc"`.

Token erzeugen (`exp`-Claim, `jwt.encode`):

```python
def create_access_token(data: dict, expires_delta: timedelta | None = None):
    to_encode = data.copy()
    if expires_delta:
        expire = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + expires_delta
    else:
        expire = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=15)
    to_encode.update({"exp": expire})
    encoded_jwt = jwt.encode(to_encode, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)
    return encoded_jwt
```

Token prüfen (`jwt.decode`, beachte `algorithms=[...]` als **Liste**):

```python
async def get_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    credentials_exception = HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
        detail="Could not validate credentials",
        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
    )
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        username = payload.get("sub")
        if username is None:
            raise credentials_exception
        token_data = TokenData(username=username)
    except InvalidTokenError:
        raise credentials_exception
    user = get_user(fake_users_db, username=token_data.username)
    if user is None:
        raise credentials_exception
    return user
```

Login-Endpoint mit Response-Modell:

```python
@app.post("/token")
async def login_for_access_token(
    form_data: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()],
) -> Token:
    user = authenticate_user(fake_users_db, form_data.username, form_data.password)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Incorrect username or password",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    access_token_expires = timedelta(minutes=ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES)
    access_token = create_access_token(
        data={"sub": user.username}, expires_delta=access_token_expires
    )
    return Token(access_token=access_token, token_type="bearer")

@app.get("/users/me/")
async def read_users_me(current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_active_user)]) -> User:
    return current_user
```

**`sub`-Claim:** laut JWT-Spec das „Subject" des Tokens; optional, aber der Ort für die User-Identifikation. Muss ein **String** und **app-weit eindeutig** sein — bei mehreren Entitätstypen präfixen, z. B. `"username:johndoe"`, um ID-Kollisionen (User `foo` vs. Car `foo`) zu vermeiden. `exp` steuert Ablauf; abgelaufener/manipulierter Token → `InvalidTokenError` → 401.

**Ablauf im Ganzen:** Passwort wird nur im ersten `/token`-Request übertragen, danach nur noch `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`. Scopes (`Security` + `SecurityScopes`) sind Thema des Advanced Guides.

# Middleware in FastAPI

FastAPI middleware processes every request before path operations handle it and every response before it's returned. According to the documentation, "A middleware is a function that works with every request before it is processed by any specific path operation."

## Creating Middleware

Middleware is created using the `@app.middleware("http")` decorator. The middleware function receives the request and a `call_next` function that passes the request to the appropriate path operation and returns its response.

## Processing Order

When multiple middlewares are added, they form a stack where the last added middleware is outermost. On requests, the outermost runs first; on responses, it runs last. For instance, if you add MiddlewareA then MiddlewareB, requests flow through B→A→route, while responses flow through route→A→B.

## Common Use Cases

Middleware can add custom headers (using the `X-` prefix) to track metrics like processing time. The documentation recommends using `time.perf_counter()` for timing accuracy.

## Execution Details

Dependencies with `yield` statements execute their exit code after middleware completes. Background tasks run after all middleware processing finishes.

# CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) { #cors-cross-origin-resource-sharing }

[CORS or "Cross-Origin Resource Sharing"](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS) refers to the situations when a frontend running in a browser has JavaScript code that communicates with a backend, and the backend is in a different "origin" than the frontend.

## Origin { #origin }

An origin is the combination of protocol (`http`, `https`), domain (`myapp.com`, `localhost`, `localhost.tiangolo.com`), and port (`80`, `443`, `8080`).

So, all these are different origins:

* `http://localhost`
* `https://localhost`
* `http://localhost:8080`

Even if they are all in `localhost`, they use different protocols or ports, so, they are different "origins".

## Steps { #steps }

So, let's say you have a frontend running in your browser at `http://localhost:8080`, and its JavaScript is trying to communicate with a backend running at `http://localhost` (because we don't specify a port, the browser will assume the default port `80`).

Then, the browser will send an HTTP `OPTIONS` request to the `:80`-backend, and if the backend sends the appropriate headers authorizing the communication from this different origin (`http://localhost:8080`) then the `:8080`-browser will let the JavaScript in the frontend send its request to the `:80`-backend.

To achieve this, the `:80`-backend must have a list of "allowed origins".

In this case, the list would have to include `http://localhost:8080` for the `:8080`-frontend to work correctly.

## Wildcards { #wildcards }

It's also possible to declare the list as `"*"` (a "wildcard") to say that all are allowed.

But that will only allow certain types of communication, excluding everything that involves credentials: Cookies, Authorization headers like those used with Bearer Tokens, etc.

So, for everything to work correctly, it's better to specify explicitly the allowed origins.

## Use `CORSMiddleware` { #use-corsmiddleware }

You can configure it in your **FastAPI** application using the `CORSMiddleware`.

* Import `CORSMiddleware`.
* Create a list of allowed origins (as strings).
* Add it as a "middleware" to your **FastAPI** application.

You can also specify whether your backend allows:

* Credentials (Authorization headers, Cookies, etc).
* Specific HTTP methods (`POST`, `PUT`) or all of them with the wildcard `"*"`.
* Specific HTTP headers or all of them with the wildcard `"*"`.

{* ../../docs_src/cors/tutorial001_py310.py hl[2,6:11,13:19] *}


The default parameters used by the `CORSMiddleware` implementation are restrictive by default, so you'll need to explicitly enable particular origins, methods, or headers, in order for browsers to be permitted to use them in a Cross-Domain context.

The following arguments are supported:

* `allow_origins` - A list of origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. E.g. `['https://example.org', 'https://www.example.org']`. You can use `['*']` to allow any origin.
* `allow_origin_regex` - A regex string to match against origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. e.g. `'https://.*\.example\.org'`.
* `allow_methods` - A list of HTTP methods that should be allowed for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `['GET']`. You can use `['*']` to allow all standard methods.
* `allow_headers` - A list of HTTP request headers that should be supported for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `[]`. You can use `['*']` to allow all headers. The `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language` and `Content-Type` headers are always allowed for [simple CORS requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#simple_requests).
* `allow_credentials` - Indicate that cookies should be supported for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `False`.

    None of `allow_origins`, `allow_methods` and `allow_headers` can be set to `['*']` if `allow_credentials` is set to `True`. All of them must be [explicitly specified](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#credentialed_requests_and_wildcards).

* `expose_headers` - Indicate any response headers that should be made accessible to the browser. Defaults to `[]`.
* `max_age` - Sets a maximum time in seconds for browsers to cache CORS responses. Defaults to `600`.

The middleware responds to two particular types of HTTP request...

### CORS preflight requests { #cors-preflight-requests }

These are any `OPTIONS` request with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` headers.

In this case the middleware will intercept the incoming request and respond with appropriate CORS headers, and either a `200` or `400` response for informational purposes.

### Simple requests { #simple-requests }

Any request with an `Origin` header. In this case the middleware will pass the request through as normal, but will include appropriate CORS headers on the response.

## More info { #more-info }

For more info about <abbr title="Cross-Origin Resource Sharing">CORS</abbr>, check the [Mozilla CORS documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS).

/// note | Technical Details

You could also use `from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware`.

**FastAPI** provides several middlewares in `fastapi.middleware` just as a convenience for you, the developer. But most of the available middlewares come directly from Starlette.

///

# SQL Databases with FastAPI: Key Patterns

## Framework Choice
The tutorial uses **SQLModel** rather than plain SQLAlchemy. As explained, "SQLModel is built on top of SQLAlchemy and Pydantic" and was created by FastAPI's author as an optimal match for the framework.

## Database & Engine Setup
The example uses SQLite with this engine configuration:
```python
engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///database.db",
    connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}
)
```

The `check_same_thread=False` parameter permits FastAPI to share the SQLite database across multiple threads within a single request.

## SessionDep Pattern
The tutorial establishes a dependency pattern using `yield`:

```python
def get_session() -> Generator[Session, None, None]:
    with Session(engine) as session:
        yield session

SessionDep = Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)]
```

This ensures "a single SQLModel session per request."

## Model Architecture
The approach uses multiple model classes through inheritance:

- **HeroBase**: Shared fields (`name`, `age`)
- **Hero** (table model): Database representation with `table=True`, includes `id` and `secret_name`
- **HeroPublic** (data model): API responses excluding sensitive `secret_name`
- **HeroCreate** (data model): Request validation, accepts `secret_name`
- **HeroUpdate** (data model): All fields optional for PATCH operations

This separation prevents clients from setting IDs and keeps sensitive data private.

## Key Operations
- **Create**: Accept `HeroCreate`, return `response_model=HeroPublic`
- **Read**: Use `select()` with pagination via `limit` and `offset`
- **Update**: Use `exclude_unset=True` with `sqlmodel_update()`
- **Delete**: Standard session deletion pattern

# Building Larger FastAPI Applications with Multiple Files

## Overview

FastAPI enables developers to structure applications across multiple files while maintaining flexibility. The framework provides `APIRouter` as a tool comparable to Flask's Blueprints for organizing code into logical modules.

## Recommended Project Structure

A typical multi-file FastAPI application follows this pattern:

```
app/
├── __init__.py
├── main.py
├── dependencies.py
└── routers/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── items.py
    └── users.py
```

Each directory containing an `__init__.py` file becomes a Python package, enabling clean imports across modules.

## Using APIRouter

`APIRouter` functions as a "mini FastAPI" class. You instantiate it similarly to the main FastAPI application:

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter()

@router.get("/users/")
async def list_users():
    ...
```

### Router Configuration Parameters

When creating an `APIRouter`, you can specify several parameters that apply to all contained path operations:

- **prefix**: Path prefix for all routes (e.g., `/items`)
- **tags**: Labels for OpenAPI documentation
- **dependencies**: Requirements executed before each operation
- **responses**: Predefined response schemas

These parameters eliminate code duplication across multiple endpoints with shared characteristics.

## Integrating Routers into Main Application

The main application file imports and includes routers using `app.include_router()`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from .routers import items, users

app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(items.router)
app.include_router(users.router)
```

## Advanced Router Inclusion

When including a router, you can override or extend its configuration without modifying the original router definition:

```python
app.include_router(
    admin.router,
    prefix="/admin",
    tags=["admin"],
    dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)],
    responses={418: {"description": "I'm a teapot"}}
)
```

This approach proves valuable when sharing code across projects—configure routers differently per application without altering the source module.

## Relative Imports

Within submodules, use relative imports to access dependencies:

```python
from ..dependencies import get_token_header  # Go up one level to app/
```

A single dot (`.`) references the current package; multiple dots navigate parent packages.

## Configuration via pyproject.toml

Specify your application entrypoint to help FastAPI tooling locate your app:

```toml
[tool.fastapi]
entrypoint = "app.main:app"
```

This eliminates repeatedly passing file paths to FastAPI commands and enables IDE extensions to discover your application automatically.

# Background Tasks in FastAPI

The documentation explains how to implement deferred operations in FastAPI applications using the `BackgroundTasks` class.

## Core Concept

According to the guide, "You can define background tasks to be run *after* returning a response." This pattern enables operations that don't require client waiting, such as email notifications or file processing.

## Implementation Steps

1. **Import and declare the parameter**: Add `BackgroundTasks` as a type-annotated parameter in your path operation function
2. **Create a task function**: Define a standard Python function (async or sync) that performs your background work
3. **Register the task**: Use the `.add_task()` method to queue the function with its arguments

The `.add_task()` method accepts the task function, positional arguments, and keyword arguments that will be passed to it.

## Advanced Features

The documentation notes that dependency injection works seamlessly with background tasks across multiple dependency levels, allowing FastAPI to merge all registered tasks automatically.

## Important Considerations

The guide distinguishes between `BackgroundTasks` (recommended for FastAPI) and `BackgroundTask` (the Starlette alternative). For heavy computational workloads requiring multi-process or distributed execution, the documentation suggests considering tools like Celery instead, which requires message queue infrastructure but offers greater scalability.

For lightweight operations within a single application instance, `BackgroundTasks` provides sufficient functionality without additional complexity.

# Metadata and Docs URLs in FastAPI

This documentation covers customizing metadata and documentation URLs in FastAPI applications.

## API Metadata Configuration

FastAPI allows you to configure several metadata fields used in the OpenAPI specification and automatic API documentation:

- **title**: The API name
- **summary**: A brief overview (OpenAPI 3.1.0+, FastAPI 0.99.0+)
- **description**: Detailed explanation supporting Markdown formatting
- **version**: Your application's version number
- **terms_of_service**: URL to service terms
- **contact**: Contact information including name, URL, and email
- **license_info**: Licensing details with name, identifier (SPDX format), or URL

## Tag Metadata

You can enhance path operation organization through `openapi_tags`, which accepts a list of dictionaries containing:

- **name** (required): Must match tags used in path operations
- **description**: Optional overview supporting Markdown
- **externalDocs**: Links to external documentation with description and required URL

The metadata order determines documentation display sequence, allowing you to override alphabetical ordering.

## URL Configuration

**OpenAPI Schema**: Served at `/openapi.json` by default; customize via `openapi_url` parameter or disable entirely with `openapi_url=None`.

**Documentation Interfaces**:
- Swagger UI: Default at `/docs`; configure with `docs_url` or disable
- ReDoc: Default at `/redoc`; configure with `redoc_url` or disable

These customizations provide flexible control over API documentation presentation and accessibility.

# Stream JSON Lines in FastAPI

The documentation explains that FastAPI (version 0.134.0+) supports streaming JSON Lines—a format where individual JSON objects are separated by newlines rather than formatted as a traditional array.

## Key Concepts

**Streaming** enables applications to send data incrementally. Instead of waiting for all items to be ready, the app transmits each item as it becomes available, allowing clients to begin processing while the server continues producing subsequent items.

**JSON Lines** format sends one JSON object per line with `application/jsonl` content type. This differs from standard JSON arrays by omitting brackets and commas between objects.

## Implementation in FastAPI

To implement JSON Lines streaming, replace `return` with `yield` in path operation functions:

```python
{* ../../docs_src/stream_json_lines/tutorial001_py310.py ln[1:24] hl[24] *}
```

For async functions with Pydantic models, declare the return type as `AsyncIterable[Item]`:

```python
{* ../../docs_src/stream_json_lines/tutorial001_py310.py ln[1:24] hl[9:11,22] *}
```

Type declarations enable FastAPI to validate, document, and serialize data efficiently using Pydantic's Rust-based serialization for better performance.

Synchronous functions use `Iterable[Item]` as the return type, while omitting type annotations allows FastAPI to use `jsonable_encoder` for JSON serialization.

## Common Applications

This approach suits streaming from AI language models, logs, telemetry, or other JSON-structured data sources. For binary data like video or audio, the documentation recommends checking advanced streaming guides.

# Server-Sent Events (SSE) in FastAPI

Server-Sent Events enable real-time data streaming from server to client using HTTP. FastAPI supports SSE through the `EventSourceResponse` class, allowing developers to stream JSON-formatted data or custom events.

## Key Implementation Details

To implement SSE, import `EventSourceResponse` from `fastapi.sse` and use `yield` in your path operation:

```python
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse

@app.get("/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def stream_data() -> AsyncIterable[Item]:
    # yield data items
```

## Core Features

**Data Formats**: You can yield plain Pydantic models (JSON-encoded automatically) or `ServerSentEvent` objects for custom SSE fields like `event`, `id`, and `retry`.

**Raw Data Support**: The `raw_data` parameter lets you send unencoded text, useful for log lines or special markers.

**Connection Resilience**: FastAPI automatically sends "keep-alive" ping comments every 15 seconds and sets appropriate headers (`Cache-Control: no-cache`, `X-Accel-Buffering: no`) to prevent proxy interference.

**Resumption**: Clients can reconnect using the `Last-Event-ID` header, allowing you to resume streaming from where the connection dropped.

**Method Flexibility**: SSE works with any HTTP method—not just GET—making it compatible with protocols like MCP that stream over POST requests.

# Summary of Static Files Documentation

This FastAPI documentation explains how to serve static files using the `StaticFiles` class.

## Key Concepts

**Basic Implementation:**
Import `StaticFiles` and mount an instance at a specific path to automatically serve files from a directory.

**What is Mounting:**
The documentation describes mounting as "adding a complete 'independent' application in a specific path, that then takes care of handling all the sub-paths." This differs from using an `APIRouter`, since mounted applications operate independently without affecting the main application's OpenAPI documentation.

**Parameters Explained:**
- The first parameter (e.g., `"/static"`) specifies the URL path where files are accessible
- The `directory` parameter names the folder containing your static files
- The `name` parameter provides an internal identifier for FastAPI

**Important Note:**
For hosting frontend applications, the documentation recommends using `app.frontend()` instead, as it leverages `StaticFiles` internally while offering additional benefits like client-side routing support.

The documentation references the code example file `../../docs_src/static_files/tutorial001_py310.py` (lines 2 and 6) and directs readers to Starlette's official documentation for more advanced options.

# FastAPI Testing Guide Summary

This documentation covers testing FastAPI applications using `TestClient`, which is based on Starlette and HTTPX.

## Key Setup Points

To begin testing, install `httpx` and import `TestClient` from FastAPI. The documentation states: "Create functions with a name that starts with `test_` (this is a standard `pytest` convention)."

Testing functions should use regular `def` declarations rather than `async def`, allowing direct pytest usage without complications.

## File Organization

For structured projects, tests can be separated into dedicated files. The guide recommends placing a `test_main.py` file within the same Python package as your application code, enabling relative imports of your FastAPI app instance.

## Testing Techniques

When sending data to your application during tests, you can:
- Add path/query parameters directly to URLs
- Pass Python objects to the `json` parameter for JSON bodies
- Use the `data` parameter for form data
- Supply headers via a `dict` in the `headers` parameter
- Include cookies through the `cookies` parameter

The documentation notes an important limitation: "the `TestClient` receives data that can be converted to JSON, not Pydantic models." For Pydantic models in tests, use `jsonable_encoder`.

## Running Tests

After installing pytest, execute your test suite using `uv run pytest`, which automatically discovers and runs all test files following pytest conventions.

# Debugging FastAPI Applications

The documentation explains how to connect a debugger to your FastAPI application using popular editors like Visual Studio Code or PyCharm.

## Direct Uvicorn Execution

You can import and run uvicorn directly within your FastAPI application file. This approach enables debugger integration since you're executing the server from your code.

## The `__name__ == "__main__"` Pattern

This conditional check ensures certain code executes only when the file runs directly:

```console
$ uv run python myapp.py
```

When invoked this way, Python sets the internal `__name__` variable to `"__main__"`, triggering the uvicorn server startup. However, when another module imports your file, this condition remains false, preventing unwanted server initialization.

## Debugger Setup

**Visual Studio Code:** Access the Debug panel, add a Python configuration, and select "Python: Current File (Integrated Terminal)" to launch the debugger.

**PyCharm:** Use the Run menu, select "Debug...", choose your file from the context menu, and the debugger launches your FastAPI server.

Both approaches allow you to set breakpoints and step through your code while the server runs. The documentation includes visual examples showing debugger interfaces for each editor.

# Frontend Serving in FastAPI

FastAPI provides `app.frontend()` to serve static frontend applications built by tools like React, Vue, Angular, and Astro.

## Basic Setup

After building your frontend (e.g., `npm run build`), place generated files in a directory like `dist/`. Then serve them:

```python
app.frontend()
```

FastAPI checks path operations first, so your API routes maintain priority over frontend files.

## Client-Side Routing

For single-page apps using client-side routing, use the fallback parameter:

```python
app.frontend(fallback="index.html")
```

This serves `index.html` for unmatched browser navigation requests, allowing your frontend framework to handle routing. However, as the documentation notes, "**FastAPI** uses this fallback only for `GET` and `HEAD` requests that explicitly accept HTML," ensuring missing static assets still return proper `404` responses.

## Automatic Fallback Behavior

By default, `fallback="auto"` automatically detects the appropriate behavior: serving `404.html` if present (for static site generators), or `index.html` for SPA routing.

## Custom 404 Pages

Serve a custom `404.html` file for missing paths:

```python
app.frontend(fallback="404.html")
```

This maintains a proper `404` status code while showing branded error pages.

## Router Integration & Security

You can add frontend files to an `APIRouter` with a prefix. Importantly, "Dependencies from the app, from an `APIRouter`, and from `include_router()` also apply to frontend responses," enabling authentication and authorization protections.

import time

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

app = FastAPI()


@app.middleware("http")
async def add_process_time_header(request: Request, call_next):
    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    process_time = time.perf_counter() - start_time
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(process_time)
    return response

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


def write_log(message: str):
    with open("log.txt", mode="a") as log:
        log.write(message)


def get_query(background_tasks: BackgroundTasks, q: str | None = None):
    if q:
        message = f"found query: {q}\n"
        background_tasks.add_task(write_log, message)
    return q


@app.post("/send-notification/{email}")
async def send_notification(
    email: str, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks, q: Annotated[str, Depends(get_query)]
):
    message = f"message to {email}\n"
    background_tasks.add_task(write_log, message)
    return {"message": "Message sent"}

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI, Header
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


items = [
    Item(name="Plumbus", price=32.99),
    Item(name="Portal Gun", price=999.99),
    Item(name="Meeseeks Box", price=49.99),
]


@app.get("/items/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def stream_items(
    last_event_id: Annotated[int | None, Header()] = None,
) -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
    start = last_event_id + 1 if last_event_id is not None else 0
    for i, item in enumerate(items):
        if i < start:
            continue
        yield ServerSentEvent(data=item, id=str(i))

from collections.abc import AsyncIterable

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class Prompt(BaseModel):
    text: str


@app.post("/chat/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def stream_chat(prompt: Prompt) -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:

    for word in words:

    yield ServerSentEvent(raw_data="[DONE]", event="done")

############ middleware.md # Middleware { #middleware } You can add middleware to **FastAPI** applications. A "middleware" is a function that works with every **request** before it is processed by any specific *path operation*. And also with every **response** before returning it. * It takes each **request** that comes to your application. * It can then do something to that **request** or run any needed code. * Then it passes the **request** to be processed by the rest of the application (by some *path operation*). * It then takes the **response** generated by the application (by some *path operation*). * It can do something to that **response** or run any needed code. * Then it returns the **response**. /// note | Technical Details If you have dependencies with `yield`, the exit code will run *after* the middleware. If there were any background tasks (covered in the [Background Tasks](background-tasks.md) section, you will see it later), they will run *after* all the middleware. /// ## Create a middleware { #create-a-middleware } To create a middleware you use the decorator `@app.middleware("http")` on top of a function. The middleware function receives: * The `request`. * A function `call_next` that will receive the `request` as a parameter. * This function will pass the `request` to the corresponding *path operation*. * Then it returns the `response` generated by the corresponding *path operation*. * You can then further modify the `response` before returning it. {* ../../docs_src/middleware/tutorial001_py310.py hl[8:9,11,14] *} /// tip Keep in mind that custom proprietary headers can be added [using the `X-` prefix](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers). But if you have custom headers that you want a client in a browser to be able to see, you need to add them to your CORS configurations ([CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)](cors.md)) using the parameter `expose_headers` documented in [Starlette's CORS docs](https://starlette.dev/middleware/#corsmiddleware). /// /// note | Technical Details You could also use `from starlette.requests import Request`. **FastAPI** provides it as a convenience for you, the developer. But it comes directly from Starlette. /// ### Before and after the `response` { #before-and-after-the-response } You can add code to be run with the `request`, before any *path operation* receives it. And also after the `response` is generated, before returning it. For example, you could add a custom header `X-Process-Time` containing the time in seconds that it took to process the request and generate a response: {* ../../docs_src/middleware/tutorial001_py310.py hl[10,12:13] *} /// tip Here we use [`time.perf_counter()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html#time.perf_counter) instead of `time.time()` because it can be more precise for these use cases. 🤓 /// ## Multiple middleware execution order { #multiple-middleware-execution-order } When you add multiple middlewares using either `@app.middleware()` decorator or `app.add_middleware()` method, each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack. The last middleware added is the *outermost*, and the first is the *innermost*. On the request path, the *outermost* middleware runs first. On the response path, it runs last. For example: ```Python app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA) app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB) ``` This results in the following execution order: * **Request**: MiddlewareB → MiddlewareA → route * **Response**: route → MiddlewareA → MiddlewareB This stacking behavior ensures that middlewares are executed in a predictable and controllable order. ## Other middlewares { #other-middlewares } You can later read more about other middlewares in the [Advanced User Guide: Advanced Middleware](../advanced/middleware.md). You will read about how to handle CORS with a middleware in the next section. ############ testing.md # Testing { #testing } Thanks to [Starlette](https://starlette.dev/testclient/), testing **FastAPI** applications is easy and enjoyable. It is based on [HTTPX](https://www.python-httpx.org), which in turn is designed based on Requests, so it's very familiar and intuitive. With it, you can use [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/) directly with **FastAPI**. ## Using `TestClient` { #using-testclient } /// note To use `TestClient`, first install [`httpx`](https://www.python-httpx.org). Add it to your project: ```console $ uv add httpx ``` /// Import `TestClient`. Create a `TestClient` by passing your **FastAPI** application to it. Create functions with a name that starts with `test_` (this is a standard `pytest` convention). Use the `TestClient` object the same way as you do with `httpx`. Write simple `assert` statements with the standard Python expressions that you need to check (again, standard `pytest`). {* ../../docs_src/app_testing/tutorial001_py310.py hl[2,12,15:18] *} /// tip Notice that the testing functions are normal `def`, not `async def`. And the calls to the client are also normal calls, not using `await`. This allows you to use `pytest` directly without complications. /// /// note | Technical Details You could also use `from starlette.testclient import TestClient`. **FastAPI** provides the same `starlette.testclient` as `fastapi.testclient` just as a convenience for you, the developer. But it comes directly from Starlette. /// /// tip If you want to call `async` functions in your tests apart from sending requests to your FastAPI application (e.g. asynchronous database functions), have a look at the [Async Tests](../advanced/async-tests.md) in the advanced tutorial. /// ## Separating tests { #separating-tests } In a real application, you probably would have your tests in a different file. And your **FastAPI** application might also be composed of several files/modules, etc. ### **FastAPI** app file { #fastapi-app-file } Let's say you have a file structure as described in [Bigger Applications](bigger-applications.md): ``` . ├── app │   ├── __init__.py │   └── main.py ``` In the file `main.py` you have your **FastAPI** app: {* ../../docs_src/app_testing/app_a_py310/main.py *} ### Testing file { #testing-file } Then you could have a file `test_main.py` with your tests. It could live on the same Python package (the same directory with a `__init__.py` file): ``` hl_lines="5" . ├── app │   ├── __init__.py │   ├── main.py │   └── test_main.py ``` Because this file is in the same package, you can use relative imports to import the object `app` from the `main` module (`main.py`): {* ../../docs_src/app_testing/app_a_py310/test_main.py hl[3] *} ...and have the code for the tests just like before. ## Testing: extended example { #testing-extended-example } Now let's extend this example and add more details to see how to test different parts. ### Extended **FastAPI** app file { #extended-fastapi-app-file } Let's continue with the same file structure as before: ``` . ├── app │   ├── __init__.py │   ├── main.py │   └── test_main.py ``` Let's say that now the file `main.py` with your **FastAPI** app has some other **path operations**. It has a `GET` operation that could return an error. It has a `POST` operation that could return several errors. Both *path operations* require an `X-Token` header. {* ../../docs_src/app_testing/app_b_an_py310/main.py *} ### Extended testing file { #extended-testing-file } You could then update `test_main.py` with the extended tests: {* ../../docs_src/app_testing/app_b_an_py310/test_main.py *} Whenever you need the client to pass information in the request and you don't know how to, you can search (Google) how to do it in `httpx`, or even how to do it with `requests`, as HTTPX's design is based on Requests' design. Then you just do the same in your tests. E.g.: * To pass a *path* or *query* parameter, add it to the URL itself. * To pass a JSON body, pass a Python object (e.g. a `dict`) to the parameter `json`. * If you need to send *Form Data* instead of JSON, use the `data` parameter instead. * To pass *headers*, use a `dict` in the `headers` parameter. * For *cookies*, a `dict` in the `cookies` parameter. For more information about how to pass data to the backend (using `httpx` or the `TestClient`) check the [HTTPX documentation](https://www.python-httpx.org). /// note Note that the `TestClient` receives data that can be converted to JSON, not Pydantic models. If you have a Pydantic model in your test and you want to send its data to the application during testing, you can use the `jsonable_encoder` described in [JSON Compatible Encoder](encoder.md). /// ## Run it { #run-it } After that, you just need to install `pytest`. Add it to your project:
```console $ uv add pytest ---> 100% ```
It will detect the files and tests automatically, execute them, and report the results back to you. Run the tests with:
```console $ uv run pytest ================ test session starts ================ platform linux -- Python 3.6.9, pytest-5.3.5, py-1.8.1, pluggy-0.13.1 rootdir: /home/user/code/superawesome-cli/app plugins: forked-1.1.3, xdist-1.31.0, cov-2.8.1 collected 6 items ---> 100% test_main.py ...... [100%] ================= 1 passed in 0.03s ================= ```
